1|78:	Viewpoint: explain a bipolar-junction transistor (BJT) used as a small‑signal amplifier (common‑emitter configuration).  1) Basic principle - A BJT controls a large collector current Ic with a much smaller base current Ib. In the active region Ic ≈ β·Ib (β = DC current gain). A small AC change in Ib produces a much larger AC change in Ic; when this varying collector current flows through a load resistor RC it produces a larger AC voltage swing at the collector: vout(t) ≈ VCC – IC(t)·RC. The result is voltage amplification with a 180° phase inversion.  2) DC biasing and Q‑point - To amplify linearly the transistor must be biased in its active region (neither saturated nor cut off). Common methods: fixed bias, emitter‑stabilized bias, and voltage‑divider bias (the most stable). Choose resistor values so the quiescent collector current ICQ and collector–emitter voltage VCEQ place the device near mid‑supply for maximum undistorted swing.  3) Small‑signal model and gain - Use the hybrid‑π or r_e' model for small AC signals. Key small‑signal parameters:   - gm ≈ ICQ / VT (VT ≈ 25 mV at 25°C).     - rπ ≈ β / gm. - Voltage gain (approx): Av ≈ vout/vin ≈ −gm · (RC || RL). The negative sign indicates phase inversion. - For emitter degeneration (unbypassed RE) Av ≈ − (RC || RL) / (re' + RE/(β+1)) ≈ − (RC || RL) / (re' + RE) (rule of thumb), where re' ≈ 25 mV / ICQ.  4) Input and output impedances - Input resistance Rin ≈ rπ + (β+1)·RE (if emitter resistor RE present; otherwise ≈ rπ). Add bias resistor network in parallel to get total Rin seen by source. - Output resistance Rout ≈ RC || ro (ro = collector output resistance; often large so Rout ≈ RC).  5) Coupling, bypassing and practical circuit blocks - Use coupling capacitors at input and output to block DC and pass AC; select cut‑off frequency fC ≈ 1/(2πRC·C) for each coupling cap with the relevant resistance. - Emitter bypass capacitor CE: when large enough it shorts RE for AC, increasing gain; when absent or partial it provides local negative feedback, increasing linearity and input resistance but reducing gain. - Biasing resistors must set DC Q‑point independently of AC coupling components.  6) Frequency response and limits - Low‑frequency roll‑off: due to coupling and bypass capacitors (high‑pass). - High‑frequency roll‑off: due to internal capacitances Cπ and Cμ (Miller effect on Cμ) and device transit frequencies; gain falls beyond a device‑dependent fβ or fT. - Avoid operation near cutoff/saturation to prevent clipping and distortion.  7) Performance tradeoffs and design notes - Higher gain often reduces bandwidth and input swing; emitter degeneration reduces distortion and stabilizes gain. - Thermal stability: use emitter resistor and negative feedback; avoid bias that lets IC vary strongly with temperature. - For larger output drive, use emitter‑follower (common‑collector) stage after CE to lower output impedance.  Summary (practical formulas) - Ic ≈ β·Ib (DC) - gm ≈ ICQ / VT - rπ ≈ β / gm - Av ≈ −gm · (RC || RL)  (or ≈ −(RC||RL)/(re' + RE) with emitter degeneration) - Rin ≈ rπ + (β+1)RE - Rout ≈ RC || ro  This gives the operating principle, how to bias and model a BJT amplifier, the key expressions for gain and impedances, and the main practical constraints (coupling/bypass, frequency limits, thermal and distortion considerations).
2|78:	Principle (core idea) - A transistor amplifies by using a small input-driven change at one terminal to control a much larger current between two other terminals. That small control signal modulates device conductivity while the power supply provides the energy for the larger output signal. For BJTs the control quantity is base current (or base-emitter voltage); for FETs it is gate-source voltage.  How it works (BJT, common-emitter viewpoint) - Biasing: the transistor is given DC bias so it sits in the active region (not cutoff, not saturation). This establishes a quiescent collector current Ic and voltages around which small signals vary. - Small-signal action: a small change in base-emitter voltage ΔVbe produces a change in base current ΔIb (and hence ΔIc ≈ β·ΔIb). In small-signal terms the device is characterized by:   - transconductance gm ≈ Ic / 26 mV (at room temperature),   - input resistance rπ ≈ β / gm. - Voltage gain (approximate): for a common-emitter with collector resistor RC and a source resistance Rs much smaller than rπ, Av ≈ −gm · RC. The minus sign indicates the output is inverted (180° phase shift). - Input and output impedances: input impedance ≈ rπ || bias network; output impedance ≈ RC (parallel r_o if considered). Current gain ≈ β (for low-frequency, neglecting loading).  How it works (FET, common-source viewpoint) - A small change in gate-source voltage ΔVgs changes the channel conductance and thus drain current ΔId. The key parameter is transconductance gm = dId/dVgs. - Voltage gain (approx): Av ≈ −gm · RD (RD = drain resistor). FETs have very high input impedance (practically infinite for ideal MOSFETs).  Practical amplifier elements - Coupling capacitors: pass AC signals between stages and block DC so biasing is preserved. - Emitter/source bypass capacitors: increase AC gain by shorting emitter/source resistance at signal frequencies. - Bias stabilization: resistor networks, emitter degeneration (Re) or feedback used to stabilize operating point vs. temperature and device variation. - Frequency response: low-frequency rolloff from coupling/bypass capacitors; high-frequency rolloff from device internal capacitances (Miller effect) and wiring — limits bandwidth. - Distortion and limits: linear amplification requires small signals around the bias point; large signals push transistor into cutoff or saturation causing clipping. Thermal effects can change Ic and must be managed.  Design rules / quick formulas - gm ≈ Ic / 26 mV. - rπ ≈ β / gm. - BJT CE voltage gain ≈ −gm·RC (if input source sees low source resistance), or more generally Av ≈ −(β·RC)/(r_in_base + Rs) in current-control terms. - FET CS voltage gain ≈ −gm·RD. - Maximum undistorted swing limited by VCE(sat) at the low end and VCC at the high end; center the quiescent point for maximum symmetric swing.  Summary (single coherent stance) A transistor amplifier uses a DC-biased transistor in its linear (active) region so a small input change controls a larger current from the power supply. Small-signal parameters (gm, rπ, β) determine gain, while bias networks, coupling/bypass capacitors, and load/resistor choices set input/output impedances, bandwidth, and linearity. Designing a practical amplifier balances gain, impedance, frequency response and thermal/stability considerations.
3|78:	A transistor amplifies by using a small input (voltage or current) to control a much larger output current supplied from a power rail. Describe below for bipolar junction transistors (BJTs)—the most common textbook amplifier—and note key differences for FETs.  Principle - A BJT is a current-controlled device: a small change in base current (ΔIB) produces a larger change in collector current (ΔIC ≈ β·ΔIB). In small-signal terms the transistor converts an input variation into an output current (transconductance behavior) which, across a load resistor, produces a larger output voltage swing. - For FETs the gate voltage controls channel conductance; gm = dID/dVGS governs the current change.  Biasing and operating point - To amplify linearly the transistor must be biased in its active region (quiescent or Q‑point) so AC swings occur around that point without clipping. - Typical biasing components: resistor networks for DC base bias, coupling capacitors to pass AC but block DC, emitter degeneration resistors for stability.  Common amplifier configurations (BJT) - Common-emitter (CE): most used for voltage gain. Input at base, output at collector. Output is phase-inverted. High voltage gain, moderate input impedance. - Common-collector (emitter follower): input at base, output at emitter. Voltage gain ≈ 1, high input impedance, low output impedance (used as buffer). - Common-base: low input impedance, high output impedance, no phase inversion; used in high-frequency stages.  Small-signal models and key formulas - Thermal voltage: VT ≈ 25 mV (at 25 °C). - Transconductance: gm ≈ IC/VT (A/V). - Emitter intrinsic resistance (small-signal): re ≈ 1/gm ≈ VT/IE (≈ 25 mV/IE). - rπ ≈ β/gm. - Approximate CE voltage gain (emitter bypassed, source Rs small): Av ≈ −gm · (RC || RL). Using β and re: Av ≈ −β · (RC || RL) / re (when input source sees base directly). - With emitter degeneration (unbypassed RE) the gain is reduced and stabilized: Av ≈ − (RC || RL) / (re + (RE/ (β+1))) ≈ −(RC||RL)/(re+RE) for large β. - Input impedance levels: CE input ≈ rπ + (β+1)RE; emitter follower input ≈ (β+1)(RE || RL) (high). - Gain–bandwidth tradeoff: gain falls at high frequency due to internal capacitances (Cπ, Cμ); for BJTs the unity‑gain freq fT limits high‑frequency performance. Gain × bandwidth is approximately constant for a stage.  Coupling, capacitors and frequency response - AC coupling capacitors (input, output) and emitter bypass capacitors set low-frequency rolloffs (high-pass behavior). Their reactances with input/output resistance set the low‑cutoff. - High-frequency rolloff caused by device capacitances and wiring, producing poles; Miller effect (Cμ) increases effective input capacitance in CE, reducing bandwidth.  Practical considerations - Set Q‑point centrally on the DC load line for maximum undistorted swing. - Use emitter degeneration for linearity and thermal stability; bypass with a capacitor if full gain is needed at AC. - Match impedances as needed (buffers, emitter followers) to avoid loading and loss of gain. - Thermal runaway: incorporate negative feedback (emitter resistor) and proper biasing to stabilize against temperature changes.  FET differences (brief) - FETs are voltage-controlled, have very high input impedance, and are often used where minimal input loading is required. Small-signal gain is governed by gm and load similar to BJTs.  Summary (practical rules) - Amplification = small input → larger output current → larger output voltage across load. - Key small-signal tools: gm, re, rπ, β. Useful approximations: gm ≈ IC/25 mV; re ≈ 25 mV / IE. - Choose CE for voltage gain, emitter follower for buffering, and apply proper biasing and coupling to achieve required gain, bandwidth and linearity.
4|78:	Viewpoint: describe a bipolar-junction transistor (BJT) used as a practical linear amplifier (common-emitter configuration).  1) Basic principle - A transistor controls a large collector current IC with a much smaller base current IB. In small-signal (linear) operation a small change in input (ΔVBE or ΔIB) produces a proportionally larger change in output current (ΔIC) so the output voltage across a load resistor is an amplified version of the input. The current gain β (≈ IC/IB) and transconductance gm (≈ IC/VT, VT ≈ 25–26 mV at 300 K) set the amplification.  2) Operating region and biasing - For linear amplification the BJT must be biased in its active region (base-emitter forward, base-collector reverse). Biasing networks set a quiescent point (Q‑point) so small signals swing symmetrically without cutoff or saturation. Typical bias measures: voltage-divider bias, emitter resistor for thermal stability, and coupling capacitors to isolate DC.  3) Small-signal model and key parameters - Small-signal parameters: gm = IC/VT, rπ = β/gm, re' ≈ 1/gm (emitter intrinsic resistance). Using the hybrid-π model, the small-signal voltage gain of a common-emitter (CE) with an emitter bypass capacitor (so emitter is at AC ground) and collector load RC is approximately:   Av ≈ −gm (RC || RL)   or, expressed with β and rπ,   Av ≈ −(β (RC || RL)) / rπ   where the minus sign indicates a 180° phase inversion.  4) Input and output impedances - Input impedance Zin ≈ rπ + (β+1)Re' (Re' is any external emitter resistance seen by AC). CE input impedance is moderate (kΩs typically). Output impedance Rout ≈ RC || ro (ro is transistor’s output resistance); CE outputs are moderate to high.  5) Frequency response - Low-frequency roll-off is set by coupling and bypass capacitors (high-pass corners from Ccouple, Cbypass interacting with resistances). High-frequency roll-off is set by transistor internal capacitances (Cπ, Cμ) and load resistances; the dominant pole often comes from Miller effect on Cμ, reducing high‑frequency gain.  6) Design and stability notes - To design: pick desired IC (sets gm), choose RC to set voltage gain and voltage swing (VCC − IC·RC leaves headroom), set emitter resistor Re for bias stability (optionally bypassed for more gain), and design bias network to set base voltage. Place coupling capacitors to block DC and choose values for required low-frequency response. - Emitter degeneration (unbypassed Re) reduces gain but improves linearity, input impedance, and thermal stability. Feedback from emitter resistor reduces distortion and stabilizes gain.  7) Performance trade-offs - Higher gain (larger RC, higher β or gm) usually reduces bandwidth and output swing. Emitter degeneration improves linearity at the cost of gain. Temperature and device variations require biasing that stabilizes IC (emitter resistor, feedback).  8) Summary formulae (useful approximations) - gm ≈ IC/VT - rπ ≈ β/gm - Voltage gain (CE, emitter bypassed): Av ≈ −gm (RC || RL) - Intrinsic emitter resistance: re' ≈ 1/gm - Input impedance ≈ rπ || bias network - Low-frequency cutoff fL from coupling capacitor C and resistance R: fL ≈ 1/(2πRC×Rseen)  This describes a practical BJT amplifier (common-emitter). FET amplifiers use the same overall idea (small gate-voltage change → larger drain current change) but differ in parameter names (transconductance gm, very high input impedance, no base current).
5|78:	A transistor amplifies by using a small input signal to control a larger current from a power supply while the device is biased in its linear (active) region. Below is a compact, practical explanation covering principle, typical circuits, key formulas and limits.  Principle - Small-signal linearization: with a steady DC bias (quiescent point) set in the active region, small changes in input (base current for a BJT, gate voltage for a FET) produce proportional changes in output current. The DC bias lets the device operate as a linear amplifier for AC signals. - Energy comes from the power supply: the transistor only controls/modulates a larger current or voltage supplied externally; it does not generate power itself.  Common configurations (purpose and basic behavior) - BJT common-emitter (CE): high voltage and power gain, 180° phase inversion (output is inverted). Widely used for voltage amplification. - BJT common-base: low input impedance, used for high-frequency gain, no phase inversion. - BJT emitter-follower (common-collector): unity (~<1) voltage gain, high input and low output impedance (buffer). - FET common-source: analogous to CE for FETs, gives voltage gain with phase inversion. - FET source-follower (common-drain): buffer, unity gain, high input impedance.  Key small-signal relations (useful approximations) - BJT:   - Current gain: β ≈ ΔIc / ΔIb.   - Transconductance: gm = Ic / VT (VT ≈ 25 mV at 25°C). Example: Ic = 1 mA → gm ≈ 40 mS.   - Input small-signal resistance at base: rπ ≈ β / gm.   - Approximate voltage gain (CE, emitter bypassed): Av ≈ −gm · (RC || ro). So Av magnitude ≈ gm·RC if ro >> RC. - FET:   - Transconductance gm = ΔId/ΔVgs.   - Approximate voltage gain (common‑source): Av ≈ −gm · (RD || ro).  Biasing and operating point - Proper DC bias sets the quiescent currents/voltages so the transistor stays in the linear region for positive and negative swings (centering on the load line). - Stabilization (resistor networks, emitter degeneration) prevents thermal runaway and sets predictable gain and input/output impedances.  Typical circuit elements for practical amplifiers - Coupling capacitors: pass AC between stages while blocking DC so biasing isn’t disturbed. - Emitter/source degeneration resistor: increases linearity and input resistance, reduces gain but stabilizes bias. - Bypass capacitor across emitter resistor: restores higher AC gain while keeping DC stabilization. - Load resistor (RC or RD) converts output current changes into output voltage changes.  Performance metrics and trade-offs - Gain: determined by gm and load (RC/RD). Higher bias current → higher gm → higher gain, but increases power dissipation. - Input impedance: low for CE, high for emitter-follower or FET gate. Design choice affects signal source loading. - Output impedance: roughly RC || device ro for voltage-output stages; low for emitter/source followers. - Bandwidth: limited by internal capacitances (Cbe, Cbc in BJTs; Cgs, Cgd in FETs) and the gain-bandwidth product (fT). Higher gain reduces usable bandwidth. - Distortion and linearity: finite β, nonlinear device characteristics and insufficient bias margin produce harmonic distortion; emitter degeneration reduces distortion. - Noise: depends on device type and bias; BJTs tend to have higher current noise, FETs higher voltage noise in some regimes.  Practical design steps (summary) 1. Choose configuration (CE, CS, emitter-follower) based on required gain and impedances. 2. Choose DC bias to set Ic (or Id) and place the quiescent point near center of the load line. 3. Select load resistor RC/RD for desired voltage swing and gain (Av ≈ −gm·RL). 4. Add coupling/bypass capacitors and degeneration resistors as needed for stability, bandwidth and linearity. 5. Check thermal stability, power dissipation and frequency response; mitigate with compensation if required.  In short: as an amplifier a transistor converts small input variations into larger output voltage/current swings by modulating a larger supply current; the small‑signal gain is set by the device transconductance and the external load, while biasing, impedance choices, and frequency effects determine real-world performance.

Design choices (configuration, bias, degeneration, coupling) set gain, impedances, linearity and bandwidth.

Use small‑signal formulas (gm = Ic/VT, rπ = β/gm, Av ≈ −gm·Rc for many CE stages) to size components and predict performance.
8|78:	Principle (summary) - A transistor amplifies by using a small input signal to control a larger current supplied by a DC source. For a BJT the small input is a base current (or base–emitter voltage) that produces a much larger change in collector current; for a FET the gate–source voltage controls the drain current. Amplification is the conversion of small input variations around a DC operating point into larger output variations.  How it’s made to work (key steps) 1. Biasing and Q‑point    - Set a DC operating point (Q‑point) in the transistor’s active region so small AC signals produce linear output variations. Common bias method: voltage‑divider bias. Proper biasing prevents cutoff or saturation during the signal swing.  2. Small‑signal operation    - Superimpose the AC input on the DC bias. Replace the transistor by its small‑signal model:      - BJT: rπ (input resistance), gm·vπ (controlled current source), ro (output resistance).      - FET: input gate high impedance, transconductance gm relates vgs → id.    - For a BJT common‑emitter (CE) amplifier with collector resistor RC: voltage gain ≈ −gm·RC (negative sign = 180° phase inversion). Using rπ, Av ≈ −β·RC/(rπ) which reduces to −gm·RC since gm = β/rπ.  3. Configurations and their characteristics    - Common‑emitter (BJT) / common‑source (FET): high voltage gain, moderate input impedance, output inverted (180°).    - Common‑collector / emitter‑follower: voltage gain ≈ 1, high input impedance, low output impedance, no phase inversion — used for buffering.    - Common‑base / source‑follower equivalent: low input impedance, no phase inversion, useful at high frequency and for current gain ≈ 1.  Practical circuit elements - Coupling capacitors: pass AC between stages while blocking DC. - Emitter (source) degeneration resistor Re: provides negative feedback → improves linearity and input impedance, reduces gain. If bypassed with capacitor at AC, gain increases at mid/high frequencies. - Load and source resistances affect gain and impedances; output typically taken across RC (or load resistor).  Performance parameters - Gain: voltage gain Av, current gain β (BJT), transconductance gm (FET/BJT small‑signal). - Input impedance Rin and output impedance Rout (design dependent). - Bandwidth: low‑frequency roll‑off from coupling/bypass capacitors; high‑frequency roll‑off from internal capacitances and Miller effect, which reduce midband gain at high frequencies. - Linearity and distortion: depend on how well Q‑point and feedback control large‑signal excursions; more emitter degeneration = lower distortion. - Noise and stability: bias networks and feedback help temperature stability; ro and bias currents introduce noise.  Design tradeoffs - Higher gain often lowers bandwidth and input impedance; feedback and emitter degeneration improve linearity and stability but reduce gain. - Choice between BJT and FET: BJT gives higher transconductance per bias current; FETs offer very high input impedance and simpler biasing for some applications.  Concise equations (useful) - Small‑signal BJT: Av ≈ −gm·RC (midband, emitter bypassed) - gm ≈ Ic / VT (VT ≈ 25 mV at room temperature) - rπ ≈ β / gm - For CE with emitter degeneration Re unbypassed: Av ≈ −gm·RC / (1 + gm·Re)  This describes how a transistor converts a small input variation into a larger output signal, the practical circuit choices to realize that, and the main performance considerations.
9|78:	Short answer A transistor amplifies by using a small input (base current or gate voltage) to control a much larger output current supplied from a power rail. Proper DC bias places the device in its active region so small AC variations about that quiescent point produce proportionally larger output variations (voltage, current or power) which, after coupling, appear as the amplified signal.  How it works (principle) - BJT: a small change in base current ΔIB produces a larger change in collector current ΔIC ≈ β·ΔIB. The transistor therefore converts small input current/voltage changes into larger output current changes; a load resistor converts that output current change into a larger output voltage swing. - FET: a small change in gate-source voltage ΔVGS modulates the channel conductance and thus drain current ΔID. The transconductance gm = dID/dVGS quantifies this conversion (voltage→current).  Key configurations and typical behavior - Common-emitter (BJT) / common-source (FET): high voltage gain, moderate input impedance, output inverted (180°). Most used for voltage amplification. - Common-collector (emitter follower) / source follower: voltage gain ≈ 1, high input and low output impedance — used as buffers. - Common-base (BJT) / common-gate (FET): low input impedance, high bandwidth, non-inverting current gain ≈ 1.  Small-signal model and important formulas (BJT focus) - Thermal voltage VT ≈ 25 mV at 300 K. - Transconductance: gm ≈ IC/VT (BJT) — units A/V. - Input resistance (base): rπ ≈ β/gm = β·VT/IC. - Output (Early) effect: ro ≈ VA/IC (often large; can be neglected for rough designs). - Approximate voltage gain (common-emitter, emitter bypassed): Av ≈ −gm·(RC || RL).     With emitter degeneration (unbypassed Re): Av ≈ −gm·(RC || RL) / (1 + gm·Re) ≈ −(RC || RL) / (re′ + Re), where re′ ≈ VT/IE. - Current gain ≈ β (BJT); input impedance ≈ rπ; output impedance ≈ RC (looking into collector, ignoring ro).  Biasing and linear operation - DC biasing sets the quiescent point (Q‑point) in the transistor’s active region so symmetric AC swings avoid cutoff or saturation. - Use voltage-divider bias and emitter resistor for thermal stability; include bypass capacitors if you want AC unbypassed behavior vs. DC stabilization.  Frequency response and practical elements - Low‑frequency rolloff: coupling capacitors (input/output) and emitter bypass capacitors form high‑pass corners; choose C·R time constants so the corner is well below the lowest signal frequency. - High‑frequency rolloff: internal capacitances (Cπ, Cμ) and the Miller effect reduce bandwidth; dominant pole often at the input node. - Tradeoff: higher gain → reduced bandwidth (gain-bandwidth product constraint).  Practical design notes and limitations - Choose Q‑point near mid‑supply for maximum symmetrical swing. - Emitter degeneration (unbypassed Re) reduces gain but improves linearity, increases input impedance and stabilizes bias. - Avoid thermal runaway: include emitter resistor and proper bias network; IC increases with temperature, changing gm and β. - Distortion arises from nonlinearity of gm and device limits; negative feedback reduces distortion and raises bandwidth.  Summary A transistor amplifier uses its transconductance/current gain to turn small input voltage/current changes into larger output current changes, which through a load produce amplified voltages. Correct DC bias, small‑signal parameter knowledge (gm, rπ, ro), coupling/bypass capacitors and attention to frequency response, thermal stability and linearity are the essentials for designing a reliable amplifier.
10|78:	Viewpoint: explain a bipolar junction transistor (BJT) used as a linear amplifier, using the common-emitter (CE) configuration as the canonical example.  Principle - A transistor converts a small input variation (base current or gate voltage) into a much larger change in output current (collector/drain current) because the device controls a large DC supply current with a small control signal. For a BJT: ΔIc ≈ β · ΔIb (β = DC current gain). This controlled collector current flowing through a load resistor produces a larger output voltage swing than the input.  DC biasing and Q‑point - To amplify linearly the transistor must be biased in its active region (not cutoff or saturation). A DC operating point (quiescent point, Q) is set by a bias network (voltage divider, emitter resistor RE, collector resistor RC, etc.). The Q‑point determines Ic, Vce and thus transistor small-signal parameters (gm, rπ, r_o).  Small‑signal model and key parameters - Transconductance: gm = Ic / VT (VT ≈ 25 mV at 25°C). gm converts input voltage change at base-emitter into collector current change: ΔIc ≈ gm·ΔVbe. - Input resistance (base): rπ ≈ β / gm = β·VT / Ic. - Output resistance: r_o ≈ VA / Ic (often large; VA is Early voltage). - These parameters form the hybrid-π small-signal model used for AC analysis.  Voltage gain, input and output impedances (CE, emitter bypassed) - With emitter bypassed (for maximum gain) and neglecting r_o, the midband voltage gain is approximately:   Av ≈ -gm · RC  (negative sign = 180° phase inversion)   or equivalently Av ≈ -β · RC / rπ. - Input resistance seen by the source: Rin(base) ≈ rπ || Rbias. If emitter resistor RE is unbypassed, Rin seen at base ≈ rπ + (β+1)RE. - Output resistance ≈ RC || r_o (typically ≈ RC).  If emitter resistor is partly or fully unbypassed - Emitting unbypassed RE reduces gain but improves linearity and increases input impedance. Approximate gain with emitter degeneration:   Av ≈ - (gm·RC) / (1 + gm·RE) ≈ -RC / (RE + r_e) for large β, where r_e ≈ 1/gm.  Frequency response - Low-frequency roll-off: set by coupling and bypass capacitors interacting with circuit resistances (fc ≈ 1/(2πRC_equiv) for each coupling/bypass network). - High-frequency roll-off: limited by internal capacitances Cπ (between base and emitter) and Cμ (base-collector). Cμ produces the Miller effect in CE, multiplying its effective input capacitance by (1 − Av), reducing bandwidth. Approximate unity‑gain bandwidth ~ gm / (2π·C_total).  Linearity and distortion - Amplification is linear only for small ΔVbe (typically a few mV). Larger signals produce nonlinear distortion because of the transistor’s exponential I-V behavior and finite output swing (limited by VCE and supply rails). Emitter degenerating resistors and feedback reduce distortion.  Practical design/analysis steps 1. Choose desired collector current Ic and supply voltage VCC. 2. Design bias network to place VCE at roughly mid-supply for maximum swing (VCE ≈ VCC/2). 3. Compute gm, rπ (from Ic and β). 4. Select RC to set required voltage gain (Av ≈ -gm·RC) while considering load and r_o. 5. Add emitter resistor RE (and bypass capacitor if needed) to control gain, bias stability, and linearity. 6. Choose coupling and bypass capacitors to place low-frequency cutoff below the lowest signal frequency. 7. Check high-frequency response (Cπ, Cμ, Miller effect) and ensure bandwidth meets requirements.  Summary - A transistor amplifier biases the device in the active region so a small input (ΔVbe or ΔIb) modulates a much larger collector current; that current flowing through a load resistor produces an amplified output voltage. Small‑signal parameters (gm, rπ, r_o, β) determine gain, input/output impedances and bandwidth. Proper biasing, emitter degeneration, and coupling components are required for stable, linear amplification with controlled frequency response.

Minimal server-side pseudocode (Lua) - Put in server.lua of a resource.  local ball = {   pos = vector3(200.0, 200.0, 40.0),   vel = vector3(0,0,0),   radius = 0.33,   inPlay = true,   lastHit = 0 } local dt = 0.05 -- 20 Hz local gravity = -9.81  Citizen.CreateThread(function()   while true do     Wait(dt*1000)     -- integrate     ball.vel = ball.vel + vector3(0,0,gravity) * dt     ball.pos = ball.pos + ball.vel * dt      -- ground bounce     local groundZ = 34.5     if ball.pos.z <= groundZ + ball.radius then       ball.pos = vector3(ball.pos.x, ball.pos.y, groundZ + ball.radius)       ball.vel = vector3(ball.vel.x * 0.9, ball.vel.y * 0.9, -ball.vel.z * 0.6) -- dampen     end      -- simple net plane collision (example netX)     local netX = 200.0     local netHalfWidth = 3.5     local netHeight = 36.5     if math.abs(ball.pos.y - 200.0) < netHalfWidth and        ball.pos.z < netHeight and        math.abs(ball.pos.x - netX) < 1.0 then       ball.vel = vector3(-ball.vel.x * 0.6, ball.vel.y * 0.6, ball.vel.z * 0.6)     end      -- broadcast to clients     TriggerClientEvent('volleyball:updateState', -1, {pos = ball.pos, vel = ball.vel, inPlay = ball.inPlay})   end end)  RegisterNetEvent('volleyball:requestHit') AddEventHandler('volleyball:requestHit', function(clientPos, clientForward, requestedForce)   local src = source   -- validate: distance check, cooldown, clamp force/angle   local dist = #(vector3(clientPos.x,clientPos.y,clientPos.z) - ball.pos)   if dist > 3.0 then return end   local now = os.time()   if now - ball.lastHit < 0.25 then return end -- anti-spam   ball.lastHit = now    -- compute hit direction and strength (server-side clamp)   local dir = vector3(clientForward.x, clientForward.y, math.max(0.2, clientForward.z))   dir = dir / #(dir)   local force = math.min(18.0, requestedForce or 10.0)   ball.vel = dir * force + ball.vel * 0.3 -- combine impulse + carry end)  Minimal client-side pseudocode (Lua) - Put in client.lua of the resource.  local netBall = {pos = vector3(0,0,0), vel = vector3(0,0,0)} local spawnedObj = nil  RegisterNetEvent('volleyball:updateState') AddEventHandler('volleyball:updateState', function(state)   netBall.pos = vector3(state.pos.x, state.pos.y, state.pos.z)   netBall.vel = vector3(state.vel.x, state.vel.y, state.vel.z) end)  Citizen.CreateThread(function()   -- spawn ball prop once   local model = GetHashKey('prop_beach_volball') -- example model   RequestModel(model); while not HasModelLoaded(model) do Wait(10) end   spawnedObj = CreateObject(model, netBall.pos.x, netBall.pos.y, netBall.pos.z, true, true, true)   NetworkSetEntityDynamic(spawnedObj, true)    while true do     Wait(50)     if spawnedObj ~= nil then       -- smooth interp (simple set to server state; for production interpolate)       SetEntityCoordsNoOffset(spawnedObj, netBall.pos.x, netBall.pos.y, netBall.pos.z, false, false, false)       SetEntityVelocity(spawnedObj, netBall.vel.x, netBall.vel.y, netBall.vel.z)     end   end end)  -- capture hit input Citizen.CreateThread(function()   while true do     Wait(0)     if IsControlJustReleased(0, 47) then -- G key as example       local ped = PlayerPedId()       local handPos = GetWorldPositionOfEntityBone(ped, GetPedBoneIndex(ped, 60309)) -- right hand bone       local forward = GetEntityForwardVector(ped)       local force = 12.0       TriggerServerEvent('volleyball:requestHit', {x=handPos.x,y=handPos.y,z=handPos.z}, {x=forward.x,y=forward.y,z=forward.z}, force)       -- optionally play local swing anim/sound     end   end end)  Practical tips  - Use server-side vector math and small fixed timesteps for determinism.  - Tune gravity/forces/damping to match the feel in the video.  - Interpolate client visuals to hide network jitter (lerp between last two server updates).  - This is more complex to stabilize and prone to desync/cheats — not recommended for competitive play. 1|77:	Short answer: Plotly's Table supports stacked header rows (pass header.values as a list of lists) but it does not support true colspan/merged header cells. To get the exact appearance in your image (multi-level headers with cells spanning multiple columns) the practical solution is to draw the bottom header row with go.Table and then overlay group headers using layout shapes + annotations (or annotations alone). That yields visually merged header cells.  Minimal example (two-row table, "Group A" spanning cols 0–1, "Group B" spanning cols 2–3):   import plotly.graph_objects as go  # data columns = ['A1', 'A2', 'B1', 'B2'] rows = [     [11, 12, 13, 14],   # first table row     [21, 22, 23, 24],   # second table row ]  # build table with only the lower-level header (subheaders) fig = go.Figure(data=go.Table(     header=dict(values=columns, align='center', height=30),     cells=dict(values=rows, align='center') ))  # overlay group headers as rectangles + centered text (paper coordinates) n = len(columns) groups = [('Group A', 0, 2), ('Group B', 2, 4)]  # (label, start_col_index, end_col_index) shapes = [] annotations = [] for label, start, end in groups:     shapes.append(dict(         type='rect',         xref='paper', yref='paper',         x0=start / n, x1=end / n,         y0=1.0, y1=1.08,               # place above the table header         fillcolor='#e8f4ff', line=dict(color='black', width=1)     ))     annotations.append(dict(         x=(start + end) / (2 * n), y=1.04,         xref='paper', yref='paper',         text=label, showarrow=False, font=dict(size=12)     ))  fig.update_layout(shapes=shapes, annotations=annotations, margin=dict(t=100))  fig.show()   Notes: - If you only need stacked headers without merged spans, you can pass header.values as a list of lists (each inner list is one header row). That will render stacked rows but will not merge cells visually. - The overlay approach uses paper coordinates and fixed column widths (assumes equal widths). For non-equal column widths you must compute x0/x1 accordingly (using columnwidths). - Adjust the y0/y1 / margin to position the overlay to match your desired look.
2|77:	Plotly 的 Table 支持“多行表头”：只要把 header.values 给成一个表格（list of lists），Plotly 会对同一行中相邻且相同的单元格做合并（以实现 colspan 效果）。下面给出一个最小可运行示例，演示如何做两行表头、并把“2018”“2019”跨列分组显示：  ```python import plotly.graph_objects as go  # 示例数据（每个列表对应一列） col_name = ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"] col_2018_q1 = [10, 20, 30] col_2018_q2 = [15, 25, 35] col_2019_q1 = [12, 22, 32] col_2019_q2 = [14, 24, 34]  fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Table(     header=dict(         # 两行表头：第一行把 2018/2019 分组（相同文本的相邻单元格会被合并）         values=[["", "2018", "2018", "2019", "2019"],                 ["Name", "Q1", "Q2", "Q1", "Q2"]],         align='center',         fill_color=['#f2f2f2'],         line_color='darkgray',         font=dict(size=12),         height=40     ),     cells=dict(         values=[col_name, col_2018_q1, col_2018_q2, col_2019_q1, col_2019_q2],         align='center'     ) )])  fig.update_layout(width=700, height=300) fig.show() ```  要点 - header.values 是一个行列表（每项是列数长度的列表）；Plotly 会对同一 header 行中相邻且文本相同的单元格进行合并，达到跨列表头效果。 - cells.values 需要按列传入（每个子列表是一列的数据）。 - 若需要更复杂的合并（非相邻合并或混合 rowSpan），可以用多个 Table traces 或在 layout 中用 annotation/shape 自行绘制头部。
3|77:	Plotly 的 Table trace 当前没有内建的 colspan/rowspan 功能。实现像你贴图那样的“多级表头”通常的做法是：用 Table 的 header 做多行显示（header.values 接受多行），然后通过在表头上叠加 shape/annotation 来“合并”若干相邻单元格的外观（画一个填充矩形并居中放置组名），从而模拟 colspan 效果。  下面给出一个最小可运行示例（py3 + plotly >= 4.x）。示例创建 3 列、两级表头，并把前两列用一个矩形和注释合并为 “Group A”：  ```python import plotly.graph_objects as go  # 数据 cols = ["col1", "col2", "col3"] rows = [     [1, 2, 3],     [4, 5, 6],     [7, 8, 9] ]  # 顶部两行表头：第一行我们把前两列留空，第三列放 Group B（Group A 通过 overlay 实现） header_values = [     ["", "", "Group B"],   # 顶部合并层（Group A 覆盖）、Group B 直接写入     ["col1", "col2", "col3"]  # 实际列名 ]  fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Table(     header=dict(         values=header_values,         align='center',         # 可以按行或按列设置颜色/线条，视 plotly 版本行为略有不同         fill_color=[['#dbe9ff']*3, ['#f7fbff']*3],         line_color='black',         font=dict(size=12),         height=30     ),     cells=dict(         values=rows,  # 每列一个列表         align='center',         fill_color='white',         line_color='black',         height=28     ) )])  # 列宽比例（paper 坐标系） col_widths = [0.3, 0.3, 0.4]  # 在 header 上方画一个矩形来模拟前两列的合并单元格外观 # 注意：y 从 0 到 1（paper），我们假设表头顶部占据 figure 上部若干高度 top_header_height = 0.12  # 顶层 header 的垂直高度（可调） y0 = 1 - top_header_height y1 = 1.0  # 计算 x 位置（paper 坐标系） x0 = 0.0 x1 = col_widths[0] + col_widths[1]  fig.add_shape(     type='rect',     xref='paper', yref='paper',     x0=x0, x1=x1, y0=y0, y1=y1,     fillcolor='#dbe9ff', line_color='#dbe9ff' )  # 在矩形中间添加组名注释 fig.add_annotation(     x=(x0 + x1) / 2,     y=(y0 + y1) / 2,     xref='paper', yref='paper',     text='Group A',     showarrow=False,     font=dict(size=12, color='black') )  # 小调整：隐藏图像多余边距以对齐表格位置（可按需改） fig.update_layout(margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=10, b=10))  fig.show() ```  要点总结 - plotly.table 支持多行 header（header.values 可传多行），但不支持原生的单元格合并（colspan/rowspan）。 - 用空字符串占位并在上层用 shapes + annotations 叠加，能视觉上实现合并效果。 - 可能需要根据列宽、表头行高做一些坐标微调以对齐边框和颜色。
4|77:	可以用两种常见方法实现多级表头：方法 A（简单多行表头，Plotly 原生支持）和方法 B（需要合并列/跨列效果时，用自定义形状 + 注释模拟真正的 colspan）。结论：Plotly 的 go.Table 支持多行 header（values 为嵌套列表），但不支持原生 colSpan；如需跨列合并必须用绘图层手工绘制。  下面给出两段精简可运行示例代码（Python + plotly）——方法 A 和方法 B。  方法 A：原生多行表头（没有真正的跨列合并） - 适合图中上下两层标题，但每个表格列都有自己底层单元格（不会物理合并列）。 ```python import plotly.graph_objects as go  header_vals = [     ["Group A", "Group A", "Group B", "Group B"],   # 第一层（视觉上是分组，但每列都有文本）     ["Name", "Age", "City", "Score"]                # 第二层（列名） ]  cells = [     ["Jim", "Jake", "Lily", "Tom"],     [18, 21, 30, 25],     ["London", "Dublin", "Paris", "Berlin"],     [90, 85, 92, 78] ]  fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Table(     header=dict(values=header_vals,                 align='center',                 fill_color=['#a6cee3','#a6cee3','#b2df8a','#b2df8a'], # 每列颜色可调                 line_color='darkslategray'),     cells=dict(values=cells, align='center') )]) fig.update_layout(width=700, height=300) fig.show() ``` 说明：第一行的 Group A/Group B 会在每个对应列上重复显示，视觉上分组但不是合并单元格。  方法 B：需要跨列合并（真正的 multi-column header） -> 隐藏 Table 的默认表头，用 layout.shapes + annotations 手工画合并单元格 ```python import plotly.graph_objects as go  # 表格主体（隐藏 header） cells = [     ["Jim", "Jake", "Lily", "Tom"],     [18, 21, 30, 25],     ["London", "Dublin", "Paris", "Berlin"],     [90, 85, 92, 78] ]  table = go.Table(     header=dict(values=["", "", "", ""],  # 隐藏原生表头文本                 fill_color='white', line_color='white'),     cells=dict(values=cells, align='center') )  fig = go.Figure(table)  # 在 layout 上用矩形和注释模拟合并表头 # 假设表格列在 x = 0..1 区间内平均分布，y 从 0..1（需要根据实际大小微调） shapes = [] annotations = []  # 第一层：Group A 跨前两列, Group B 跨后两列 groups = [("Group A", 0.0, 0.5), ("Group B", 0.5, 1.0)]  # (文本, x0, x1) for text, x0, x1 in groups:     shapes.append(dict(type="rect",                        xref="paper", yref="paper",                        x0=x0, x1=x1, y0=0.88, y1=1.0,                        line=dict(color='black'),                        fillcolor='#d9f0ff'))     annotations.append(dict(x=(x0 + x1)/2, y=0.94, xref='paper', yref='paper',                             text=text, showarrow=False, font=dict(size=14)))  # 第二层：列名（四列） col_count = 4 for i, col_name in enumerate(["Name", "Age", "City", "Score"]):     x0 = i/col_count     x1 = (i+1)/col_count     shapes.append(dict(type="rect",                        xref="paper", yref="paper",                        x0=x0, x1=x1, y0=0.76, y1=0.88,                        line=dict(color='black'),                        fillcolor='#ffffff'))     annotations.append(dict(x=(x0 + x1)/2, y=0.82, xref='paper', yref='paper',                             text=col_name, showarrow=False))  fig.update_layout(shapes=shapes, annotations=annotations,                   margin=dict(t=120,b=20), width=800, height=350) fig.show() ``` 说明：用 shapes（矩形）画出跨列的头单元格，再用 annotations 放文字。需要根据表格宽度/高度和列数微调 x/y 坐标与 margin。  建议 - 如果只要视觉上的多层标题（不需要真实合并单元格或交互），方法 A 简单快捷。 - 如果必须实现跨列合并（colspan）、精确样式或复杂布局，使用方法 B（自绘 header）或直接用 HTML 表格（Dash + html.Table）更灵活。  需要的话我可以把方法 B 的坐标计算通用化成一个函数，按列宽自动生成精确合并头。
5|77:	Plotly 的 go.Table 支持多行表头（header 的 values 作为多行列表），但不支持原生的 colspan/rowspan。要做出类似图片的“跨列合并”效果，有两种常用方法：  1) 简单方法（多行表头但不合并，只是重复上层标签） - 用 header.values 传入多个 header 行（每行长度等于列数），上层分组标签在每列重复显示（视觉上不是真正合并，但快速实现）。  示例： ```python import plotly.graph_objects as go  fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Table(     header=dict(         values=[             ["Group A", "Group A", "Group B", "Group B"],  # 上层（重复）             ["A1", "A2", "B1", "B2"]                        # 下层         ],         align='center', fill_color='#f2f2f2'     ),     cells=dict(         values=[             ['a11','a12'], ['a21','a22'], ['b11','b12'], ['b21','b22']         ]     ) )]) fig.show() ```  2) 进阶方法（视觉上合并单元格）——模拟 colspan - 使用 go.Table 只渲染真正的最下层列名（例如 A1,A2,B1,B2），然后通过 layout 的 shapes（矩形）和 annotations 在表格上方绘制合并的上层标签（跨越若干列的矩形并在中间放置文本）。这是目前在 Plotly 中实现跨列合并（视觉上）最可靠的办法。  示例（Group A 跨前两列，Group B 跨后两列）： ```python import plotly.graph_objects as go  # 表格数据（每项为一列） cells = [     ['A1_row1', 'A1_row2'],     ['A2_row1', 'A2_row2'],     ['B1_row1', 'B1_row2'],     ['B2_row1', 'B2_row2'] ]  ncols = 4 colw = 1.0 / ncols  fig = go.Figure()  # 只绘制二级列名（真实列头） fig.add_trace(go.Table(     header=dict(values=["A1", "A2", "B1", "B2"], align='center', fill_color='#ffffff'),     cells=dict(values=cells) ))  # 在表上方绘制两个跨列矩形并添加文字（使用 paper 坐标系） shapes = [     dict(type="rect", xref='paper', yref='paper',          x0=0, x1=colw*2, y0=0.95, y1=1.0, fillcolor='#e8f4ff', line=dict(color='#b3d7ff')),     dict(type="rect", xref='paper', yref='paper',          x0=colw*2, x1=1.0, y0=0.95, y1=1.0, fillcolor='#e8f4ff', line=dict(color='#b3d7ff')) ] fig.update_layout(shapes=shapes, margin=dict(t=80))  # 添加上层合并文字，居中于各自区域 fig.add_annotation(x=colw*(0+2)/2, y=0.975, xref='paper', yref='paper',                    text="Group A", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=12)) fig.add_annotation(x=colw*(2+4)/2, y=0.975, xref='paper', yref='paper',                    text="Group B", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=12))  fig.show() ```  建议 - 如果能接受重复显示上层标签，第一种方式最快；若需要真视觉上的合并（跨列大标题），用第二种方法（shapes + annotations）来自行绘制上层 header。 - 根据实际列宽和表格在画布中的位置，可能需调整 shapes 的 y0/y1、margin 和 annotation 的 y 值以对齐。
6|77:	可以用 plotly.graph_objects.Table 通过把表头传成“多行”的 values 来模拟多级表头（用空字符串占位表示跨列），示例如下；注意 Plotly Table 没有真正的 colspan/rowspan，因此这是视觉上的合并；若需要完全控制边框/跨列行为，建议用 HTML 表格（Dash）或用 heatmap + annotations + shapes 自行绘制。  示例代码（可直接运行）：  ```python import plotly.graph_objects as go  fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Table(     header=dict(         # 每个子列表是一行表头；用 '' 占位模拟合并单元格         values=[             ['<b>Group A</b>', '', '<b>Group B</b>'],   # 顶层             ['Sub A1', 'Sub A2', 'Sub B1']              # 次级         ],         align='center',         line_color='darkslategray',         fill_color='lightgrey',         height=40     ),     cells=dict(         values=[             ['Jim Red', 'Jake White', 'Alice Blue'],    # 列1 列2 列3 的数据             [18, 18, 30],             ['London', 'Dublin', 'Paris']         ],         align='center'     ) )])  fig.update_layout(width=700, height=320, margin=dict(t=20,b=20)) fig.show() ```  要点 - header.values 接受多行（list of lists），每个内层列表对应一行表头； - 使用空字符串 '' 来占位以“合并”上方单元格（视觉效果），但内部边框不能按单元格自由隐藏； - 如果需要真实的 colspan/rowspan 或更精细的边框控制，推荐用 HTML Table（在 Dash/Notebook 中）或用 plotly 的 shapes + annotations 自行绘制表头。
7|77:	可以用 Plotly 的 go.Table 通过给 header.values 传入多行列表来模拟多级表头；对于跨列合并（colspan）Plotly 没有原生 rowspan/colspan 支持，常用技巧是把被合并位置用空字符串占位并用相同的背景色/隐藏分割线来“伪装”合并单元格，或者使用 HTML 表格（Dash/Flask）来获得真实 colspan/rowspan。下面给出一个可直接运行的最常用做法（伪合并）示例：  示例代码（Python + plotly）： ``` import plotly.graph_objects as go  # 顶层和次级表头（用空字符串占位模拟合并） header_values = [     ["Group A", "", "Group B", "Group C", ""],   # 顶层（合并看起来是 Group A 跨两列，Group C 跨两列）     ["A1", "A2", "B1", "C1", "C2"]               # 次级表头 ]  # 示例数据列 cols = [     ["a1","a2","a3"],  # A1 列     ["b1","b2","b3"],  # A2 列     ["c1","c2","c3"],  # B1 列     ["d1","d2","d3"],  # C1 列     ["e1","e2","e3"],  # C2 列 ]  fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Table(     header=dict(         values=header_values,         align='center',         # 两行 header 分别设置背景色（二维列表），使占位空单元格与上层单元格同色，从视觉上合并         fill_color=[['#d9e6f6']*5, ['#f7fbff']*5],         font=dict(size=12),         line_color='gray'     ),     cells=dict(         values=cols,         align='center'     ) )])  fig.update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=10,b=10)) fig.show() ```  要点与限制 - header.values 接受多行列表，可实现多行表头（multi-row header）。 - Plotly Table 没有真实的 colspan/rowspan：用空字符串占位 + 统一填充色、匹配边框色可以“伪装”合并，但不能完全删除单元格边框或实现复杂的跨行跨列行为。 - 若需要严格的 colspan/rowspan（像 HTML 表格那样），推荐使用 HTML 表格（在 Dash 中直接写 <table> 或用 dash_table.DataTable 的 style 定制），或把多层表头用多个 Table traces / annotations / shapes 组合来精细控制布局。
8|77:	Plotly's go.Table accepts header.values as a list-of-rows (so you can show multiple header rows), but it does not support true colspan/rowspan. To get the exact "merged" multi-level header look you must either repeat group labels across columns or visually emulate colspan by drawing shapes/annotations above the table. I recommend the latter for a clean multi-level header.  Minimal two-row header (no real colspan): ``` import plotly.graph_objects as go  fig = go.Figure(go.Table(     header=dict(values=[         ["Group 1", "Group 1", "Group 2", "Group 2"],   # first header row         ["Name", "Age", "City", "Country"]              # second header row     ],     align='center', fill_color='paleturquoise'),     cells=dict(values=[         ["Jim", "Jake"],         [18, 18],         ["London", "Dublin"],         ["UK", "IE"]     ],     align='center')) )) fig.show() ``` This shows two header rows but repeats the group label per column.  Emulated colspan (drawn group boxes above the table): ``` import plotly.graph_objects as go  # table data header2 = ["Name", "Age", "City", "Country"] cells = [["Jim", "Jake"], [18, 18], ["London", "Dublin"], ["UK", "IE"]]  fig = go.Figure(go.Table(     header=dict(values=[header2], fill_color='white', align='center', height=30),     cells=dict(values=cells, align='center') ))  # define groups as (label, first_col_index, last_col_index) groups = [("Group 1", 0, 1), ("Group 2", 2, 3)] ncols = len(header2) col_w = 1.0 / ncols  shapes = [] annotations = [] for label, i, j in groups:     x0 = i * col_w     x1 = (j + 1) * col_w     # rectangle above the table (paper coordinates)     shapes.append(dict(type="rect", xref="paper", yref="paper",                        x0=x0, x1=x1, y0=1.0, y1=1.09,                        fillcolor="lightblue", line=dict(width=1)))     annotations.append(dict(x=(x0 + x1) / 2, y=1.045, xref="paper", yref="paper",                             text=label, showarrow=False, font=dict(size=12)))  fig.update_layout(     shapes=shapes,     annotations=annotations,     margin=dict(t=100),  # give space for the group boxes     height=300 ) fig.show() ``` Notes: - Use paper coordinates to place shapes/annotations relative to the whole figure; compute column widths as 1/number_of_columns. - Adjust y0/y1, margin.t and header.height to tune spacing. - This approach visually replicates colspan even though Plotly Table has no native colspan/rowspan.
9|77:	You can create multi-row headers in Plotly by giving header.values as a list of rows (each inner list must have one entry per final column). Plotly Table does not support true colspan/rowspan, but you can visually mimic merged header cells by repeating the group label across the grouped columns and hiding the inner vertical borders (or overlaying annotations/shapes).  Minimal example (Group A spans columns 2–3, Group B spans 4–5):   import plotly.graph_objects as go  # top row repeats group labels for columns that belong to the group header_values = [     ['', 'Group A', 'Group A', 'Group B', 'Group B'],     ['Name', 'Age', 'City', 'Phone', 'Email'] ]  cells_values = [     ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'],        # Name     [24, 30, 22],                       # Age     ['NY', 'LA', 'SF'],                 # City     ['123-111', '456-222', '789-333'],  # Phone     ['a@x.com', 'b@y.com', 'c@z.com']   # Email ]  fig = go.Figure(go.Table(     header=dict(         values=header_values,         align='center',         # try to hide inner vertical borders (transparent where you want a merged look)         line_color=['black', 'rgba(0,0,0,0)', 'black', 'rgba(0,0,0,0)', 'black'],         fill_color='lightgrey',         font=dict(size=12)     ),     cells=dict(values=cells_values, align='left') ))  fig.update_layout(width=800, height=320) fig.show()   Notes - header.values is a list of header-rows; each inner list length must equal number of columns. - There is no native colSpan/rowSpan in Plotly Table. The shown technique repeats group labels and hides inner borders to simulate spans. For perfect merged cells you can also overlay annotations and shapes in the layout to draw a single label spanning multiple columns.
10|77:	简短回答（可直接运行的示例）：Plotly 的 go.Table 支持多行表头（将 header.values 设为 list of lists），但不原生支持 colspan/rowspan 的真正单元格合并。常用的两种做法：  - 如果只是“多行表头（每列有多级名称）”，直接用多行 header.values。 - 如果需要“表头横向合并（colspan）”的视觉效果，可把第一行的合并单元格在相邻列只写一次文字并把那些空单元格填成相同背景色，或更精确地用 layout.shapes/annotations 在表格上方画合并的矩形。  下面给出两段代码：第一段演示多行表头；第二段演示通过留空并统一填色来模拟 colspan 的方法（常用且简单）。  示例 1：多行表头（stacked headers） ```python import plotly.graph_objects as go  # 两行表头：第一行为大类，第二行为具体列名 header_values = [     ["Group A", "Group A", "Group B", "Group B", "Group B"],     ["Name", "Age", "S1", "S2", "S3"] ]  # 按列给出单元格数据 cells = [     ["Jim", "Jake", "Amy"],      # Name     [18, 19, 17],                # Age     [88, 92, 79],                # S1     [90, 85, 88],                # S2     [75, 80, 82],                # S3 ]  fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Table(     header=dict(         values=header_values,         align='center',         fill_color=[["#e6f7ff"]*5, ["#ffffff"]*5],  # 两行表头分别颜色         line_color='black',         height=40     ),     cells=dict(         values=cells,         align='center',         fill_color=[["#fafafa"]*5]*len(cells),         line_color='black'     ) )]) fig.update_layout(width=800, height=300) fig.show() ```  示例 2：模拟 colspan（在第一行仅显示一次文字并把相邻空单元格填成相同颜色） ```python import plotly.graph_objects as go  header_values = [     ["Group A", "", "Group B", "", ""],   # 通过空字符串模拟合并     ["Name", "Age", "S1", "S2", "S3"] ]  # 指定第一行每个单元格背景（用相同颜色让 Group A 看起来是合并的） header_fill = [     ["#cfeef8", "#cfeef8", "#fce8cf", "#fce8cf", "#fce8cf"],  # 第一行背景 per cell     ["#ffffff", "#ffffff", "#ffffff", "#ffffff", "#ffffff"]   # 第二行背景 ]  cells = [     ["Jim", "Jake", "Amy"],     [18, 19, 17],     [88, 92, 79],     [90, 85, 88],     [75, 80, 82], ]  fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Table(     header=dict(         values=header_values,         align='center',         fill_color=header_fill,         line_color='black',         height=40     ),     cells=dict(values=cells, align='center') )]) fig.update_layout(width=800, height=300) fig.show() ```  如果需要完全精确的合并（没有单元格间的边线、文字居中跨列），建议用第二种方法再配合 layout.shapes 和 annotations 在表格上方画矩形/文字（可以精确控制跨列宽度和边框），那是实现“视觉上完全合并”的稳妥办法。
