Set your bot webhook to https://<your-app>.herokuapp.com/<TOKEN> before deploying.  main.go package main  import (  "bytes"  "encoding/json"  "log"  "net/http"  "os"  "strings"   "github.com/gin-gonic/gin" )  type Update struct {  UpdateID int     `json:"update_id"`  Message  Message `json:"message"` }  type Message struct {  MessageID int    `json:"message_id"`  From      User   `json:"from"`  Chat      Chat   `json:"chat"`  Text      string `json:"text"` }  type User struct {  ID        int64  `json:"id"`  FirstName string `json:"first_name"`  Username  string `json:"username"` }  type Chat struct {  ID   int64  `json:"id"`  Type string `json:"type"` }  type sendMessageReqBody struct {  ChatID int64  `json:"chat_id"`  Text   string `json:"text"` }  func main() {  token := os.Getenv("TELEGRAM_TOKEN")  if token == "" {   log.Fatal("TELEGRAM_TOKEN not set")  }  port := os.Getenv("PORT")  if port == "" {   port = "3000"  }   gin.SetMode(gin.ReleaseMode)  r := gin.Default()   // Use the token in the path to keep endpoint secret-ish  hookPath := "/" + token  r.POST(hookPath, func(c *gin.Context) {   var upd Update   if err := c.ShouldBindJSON(&upd); err != nil {    c.Status(http.StatusBadRequest)    return   }   text := strings.ToLower(upd.Message.Text)   if strings.Contains(text, "marco") {    if err := sayPolo(token, upd.Message.Chat.ID); err != nil {     log.Println("send error:", err)    }   }   c.Status(http.StatusOK)  })   log.Println("listening on port", port)  if err := r.Run(":" + port); err != nil {   log.Fatal(err)  } }  func sayPolo(token string, chatID int64) error {  reqBody := &sendMessageReqBody{   ChatID: chatID,   Text:   "Polo!!",  }  reqBytes, err := json.Marshal(reqBody)  if err != nil {   return err  }  url := "https://api.telegram.org/bot" + token + "/sendMessage"  res, err := http.Post(url, "application/json", bytes.NewReader(reqBytes))  if err != nil {   return err  }  defer res.Body.Close()  if res.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {   return &httpError{Status: res.Status}  }  return nil }  type httpError struct{ Status string } func (e *httpError) Error() string { return "unexpected status: " + e.Status }  How to set webhook (one-time, replace <TOKEN> and <APP>): curl "https://api.telegram.org/bot<TOKEN>/setWebhook?url=https://<APP>.herokuapp.com/<TOKEN>"  Notes: - Heroku requires your app to bind to $PORT. 2|85:	Here is a minimal, practical Go webhook bot you can deploy to Heroku. It uses the plain net/http server (works the same as a small Gin server) and replies to messages containing “marco” with “Polo!!” and to the /hello command.  Save as main.go:  ```go package main  import (  "bytes"  "encoding/json"  "log"  "net/http"  "os"  "strings" )  type Update struct {  Message *Message `json:"message"` } type Message struct {  Chat Chat   `json:"chat"`  Text string `json:"text"` } type Chat struct {  ID int64 `json:"id"` }  var botToken string  func sendMessage(chatID int64, text string) error {  reqBody := map[string]interface{}{   "chat_id": chatID,   "text":    text,  }  b, err := json.Marshal(reqBody)  if err != nil {   return err  }  res, err := http.Post("https://api.telegram.org/bot"+botToken+"/sendMessage", "application/json", bytes.NewBuffer(b))  if err != nil {   return err  }  defer res.Body.Close()  if res.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {   return &httpError{res.Status}  }  return nil }  type httpError struct{ s string } func (e *httpError) Error() string { return e.s }  func webhookHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {  var upd Update  if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&upd); err != nil {   w.WriteHeader(http.StatusBadRequest)   return  }  if upd.Message == nil {   w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)   return  }   text := strings.ToLower(upd.Message.Text)   if strings.Contains(text, "marco") {   _ = sendMessage(upd.Message.Chat.ID, "Polo!!")  }  if strings.HasPrefix(upd.Message.Text, "/hello") {   _ = sendMessage(upd.Message.Chat.ID, "Hello!")  }  w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK) }  func main() {  botToken = os.Getenv("BOT_TOKEN")  if botToken == "" {   log.Fatal("BOT_TOKEN env var required")  }  port := os.Getenv("PORT")  if port == "" {   port = "3000"  }   http.HandleFunc("/webhook", webhookHandler)  log.Println("listening on port", port)  log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":"+port, nil)) } ```  How to use - Locally: set BOT_TOKEN and run: BOT_TOKEN=xxxx go run main.go - Deploy to Heroku: set BOT_TOKEN as a config var, push the app (Heroku will provide PORT). - Register webhook: after deploying, run:   https://api.telegram.org/bot<YOUR_BOT_TOKEN>/setWebhook?url=https://<your-app>.herokuapp.com/webhook  This is intentionally minimal; for more features (routing, file uploads, command handlers) you can switch to a library such as telego or go-telegram/bot and use Gin for more elaborate web handling as shown in the linked resources.

Concrete roadmap and options:  1. Quick start — BasicEffect (fastest) - Use BasicEffect to get ambient/diffuse/specular and up to 3 directional lights with almost no shader work:   - Set World/View/Projection matrices.   - enable Lighting and set AmbientLightColor, PreferPerPixelLighting = true, and configure DirectionalLight0..2 (Direction, DiffuseColor, SpecularColor). - Good for prototyping, low complexity, modest quality.  2. Advanced — deferred shading (many lights) - Render a G‑buffer (albedo, normal, world position or depth+reconstruct, material params) into MRTs. - In a full‑screen pass, accumulate lights using the G‑buffer (fast for many lights). - Add tiled/clustered lighting for even better scalability.  4. Shadows & other effects - Shadow mapping for directional/spot/point lights (PCF or cascaded shadow maps for large scenes). - SSAO (screen-space ambient occlusion) for contact shadows. - Reflection probes / environment maps for specular reflections. - Postprocess (tone mapping, bloom) for final look.  5. Practical MonoGame tips - Use MonoGame Effect (.fx -> .mgfx) compiled through the Pipeline tool. - For HLSL, write shaders targeting the correct profile (GL/DX differences if cross-platform). - Keep per‑draw constants minimal; update buffers or effect parameters efficiently. - Profile and batch geometry; prefer GPU instancing for many similar objects.  Example (BasicEffect skeleton): effect.World = world; effect.View = view; effect.Projection = projection; effect.EnableDefaultLighting(); // sets 3 directional lights and ambient effect.PreferPerPixelLighting = true; effect.DiffuseColor = new Vector3(1,1,1); // material color  If you want one concrete next step: implement a simple per‑pixel effect with albedo + normal map (Phong) — it yields a big visual improvement for little complexity before tackling deferred rendering or shadows.

Practical roadmap  1) Pick a lighting model - Start with Blinn–Phong per-pixel (diffuse + specular + ambient). MonoGame will handle cross-compilation for platforms. - Pass standard parameters: World, View, Projection, NormalMatrix (world inverse-transpose), camera position, light positions/colors, material properties, textures.  4) Essentials in the shader - Transform normals correctly: use world inverse-transpose for normals or compute TBN for tangent-space normal maps. - Compute lighting per-pixel in the pixel shader: L = ambient + diffuse * max(N·L,0) + specular * pow(max(R·V,0), shininess). - For normal mapping, supply tangent/bitangent in vertex data and sample a normal map in tangent space.  5) Shadows & advanced effects - Shadow mapping: render scene depth from light into a depth map, sample in main shader to test occlusion. - SSAO, bloom, tonemapping, HDR for higher quality. - For many lights use deferred shading (albedo, normal, position/depth buffers), then light accumulation pass.  6) Implementation notes / performance - Use Content.Load<Effect>("MyShader") to load shaders. - Update Effect parameters every frame (matrices, lights). - Convert colors/textures to linear space for correct lighting; apply gamma correction/tonemapping on output. - Limit per-object state changes, batch meshes, and profile; deferred costs more memory but scales with light count.  Minimal code sketch (C#): effect = Content.Load<Effect>("Phong"); effect.Parameters["World"].SetValue(world); effect.Parameters["View"].SetValue(view); effect.Parameters["Projection"].SetValue(proj); effect.Parameters["LightDirection"].SetValue(lightDir); effect.Parameters["LightColor"].SetValue(lightColor.ToVector3()); effect.Parameters["CameraPos"].SetValue(cameraPosition);  Then draw your mesh with that effect applied.  Learning path - Try BasicEffect first for built-in simple lighting. - Write a small per-pixel Blinn–Phong Effect to learn shader parameters. - Add normal maps, then shadow mapping, and finally consider deferred/PBR when you need many lights or high realism.  References: MonoGame Effects documentation, HLSL/GLSL shader tutorials, normal mapping and shadow mapping guides.

Common families are: - Linear models (logistic regression), maximum‑margin SVMs, - Tree‑based methods (decision trees, random forests, bagging/boosting like XGBoost), - Instance‑based (k‑NN), - Neural networks / deep learning.  When to use which - Start with simple, interpretable models (logistic regression, decision trees) for small data or when explainability matters. - Use tree ensembles (random forest, gradient boosting) for tabular data with nonlinearities and heterogeneous features. - Use deep networks for very large data or complex unstructured inputs (images, audio, text).  Practical, evidence‑based guidance - Feature choice and sampling strongly affect performance (e.g., remote‑sensing LULC studies show training sampling design changes accuracy). - Ensembles often improve robustness: a bagged decision‑tree ensemble outperformed alternatives in automatic prominent‑syllable detection (accuracy ≈ 95.9%). - Compare a set of models (logistic regression, RF, XGBoost, DNN) and validate on external/multi‑center data when possible (medical mortality prediction used 12–18 variables across centers). - Always handle class imbalance, scale/encode features appropriately, use cross‑validation and hyperparameter tuning, and report multiple metrics (accuracy, F1, AUC, Cohen’s κ).  Limitations - Susceptible to overfitting, domain shift, and poor data quality; interpretability decreases with model complexity.  Recommendation For most practical problems, baseline with logistic regression and a tree ensemble (random forest/XGBoost), tune via cross‑validation, address sampling/design issues, and externally validate before deployment.
2|96:	A concise, practical summary of machine‑learning classifiers and how to use them  What they are - Supervised models that predict a discrete label from input features (e.g., spam/not‑spam, land‑cover class, prominent syllable, postoperative mortality).  Common algorithms - Linear: logistic regression. Good baseline, interpretable. - Margin methods: support vector machines (SVM). Good for medium‑sized, well‑scaled data. - Tree‑based: decision trees, random forest, gradient‑boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM). Strong off‑the‑shelf performance, handle mixed features, give feature importance. - Instance‑based: k‑nearest neighbors. Simple but scales poorly with data. - Neural nets / deep learning: best for very large, high‑dimensional inputs (images, speech). - Ensembles: bagging and boosting often outperform single learners (e.g., bagged trees gave top results in syllable detection).  Typical workflow / best practices 1. Define target and realistic evaluation metric (accuracy, precision/recall, F1, AUC, Cohen’s κ). 2. Clean and preprocess: handle missing values, encode categoricals, scale as needed. 3. Design sampling and train/test splits carefully (stratify, avoid leakage; sampling design affects performance). 4. Start with a simple baseline (logistic regression); then try tree ensembles and SVMs; use deep models only if data and problem justify them. 5. Use k‑fold cross‑validation and proper hyperparameter tuning (grid/random/ Bayesian). 6. Address class imbalance (resampling, class weights, threshold tuning, appropriate metrics). 7. Validate on independent / multi‑center data for generalization (important in medicine, remote sensing). 8. Inspect feature importance and model errors; calibrate probabilities if needed.  Common pitfalls - Overfitting (insufficient validation, overly complex models). - Data leakage (features derived from the future/target). - Poor sampling design leading to optimistic results. - Ignoring class imbalance and using inappropriate metrics.  Recommendation (practical stance) - Use interpretable baselines; then prioritize tree‑based ensembles (random forest / XGBoost) for tabular tasks because they balance performance, robustness, and diagnostic tools. Reserve deep learning for large labeled datasets or unstructured inputs. Rigorously validate with cross‑validation and independent test sets, and report metrics appropriate to the application (e.g., F1 and Cohen’s κ in imbalanced or expert‑annotated problems).
3|96:	A concise, practical summary and guidance for machine learning classifiers (applied viewpoint)  What they are - Supervised models that assign discrete labels to inputs by learning patterns from labeled examples (classification vs. regression).  Common algorithms (and when they work well) - Logistic Regression / Linear Models: simple, fast, interpretable; good when relationships are roughly linear or features are high-dimensional and sparse. - Support Vector Machines (SVM): effective for medium-sized problems, good margin-based separation; use kernels for nonlinearity. - Decision Trees: interpretable, handle mixed data and missing values; prone to overfitting on small data. - Random Forests / Bagging: robust, low tuning, excellent for tabular data; ensembles reduce variance (e.g., bagged trees achieved top results in prosody/syllable detection). - Gradient Boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM): state-of-the-art for many tabular problems; higher accuracy but more tuning and training time. - k-Nearest Neighbors: simple, nonparametric; suitable for low-dimensional data and small datasets. - Naive Bayes: fast, works well on text and independently distributed features. - Neural Networks / Deep Learning: best for large datasets and unstructured data (images, audio, text); higher data and compute needs.  Key model-evaluation metrics - Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score for class-wise performance. - ROC AUC for ranking ability; PR AUC when classes are imbalanced. - Cohen’s kappa for agreement beyond chance (used in prosody studies). - Use confusion matrices to inspect error types.  Best practices / workflow 1. Define task and gather representative labeled data (sample design matters for remote-sensing/LULC). 2. Feature engineering and preprocessing: handle missing values, scale numeric features, encode categoricals, extract domain features (pitch/intensity/duration for speech). 3. Baseline with simple models (logistic, tree); progress to ensembles or deep models as needed. 4. Use cross-validation and a held-out test set for honest evaluation; perform hyperparameter tuning (grid/Bayesian search). 5. Address class imbalance (resampling, class weights, focal loss). 6. Monitor overfitting (learning curves, validation loss) and use regularization or ensembling. 7. Consider interpretability (shap, feature importances) and operational constraints (latency, memory).  Choosing a classifier (practical rules) - Small tabular datasets: tree ensembles (Random Forest / Gradient Boosting). - High-dimensional sparse data (text): linear models or Naive Bayes. - Large labeled unstructured data (images, speech): deep neural networks. - Need interpretability: logistic regression or shallow trees; explain ensembles with post-hoc methods. - Limited compute or quick prototyping: logistic regression / small trees / k-NN.  Trade-offs to weigh - Accuracy vs. interpretability; performance vs. training/inference cost; model complexity vs. required data volume. - Ensembles/boosting often give best accuracy on tabular tasks but require careful tuning and more compute.  Final recommendation - Start simple, validate rigorously, and escalate model complexity only when justified by data size, problem difficulty, or clear gains from validation metrics.

They learn decision boundaries from labeled training data.  - Common families and when to use them:   - Linear models (logistic regression): simple, fast, interpretable; good baseline.   - Margin methods (SVMs): effective with clear margins; need feature scaling; good for medium‑size problems.   - Tree‑based (decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting/XGBoost): handle mixed feature types, robust to outliers, provide feature importance; Practical rule of thumb: baseline with a simple model, preprocess carefully, use cross‑validation and appropriate metrics, then try tree ensembles or gradient boosting as strong general-purpose classifiers; move to deep learning only when input structure and data volume justify it.

How to choose (practical rules):   - Start with simple, interpretable baselines (logistic regression, decision tree).   - If performance is insufficient, try tree ensembles or gradient boosting.   - Use deep learning only when you have large labeled datasets or complex inputs (images, raw audio, text).   - Consider interpretability/regulatory needs (favor simpler or explainable models in medicine, finance).  - Key implementation points / best practices:   - Preprocess: handle missing values, encode categorical variables, scale features when required (SVM, k-NN, neural nets).   - Practical summary and guidance - Core idea: train on labeled examples, validate on unseen data, and measure performance with class-appropriate metrics (not just accuracy). - Common classifiers and when to try them:   - Logistic regression: simple, interpretable, strong baseline for linearly separable problems.   - Decision trees: interpretable, handle mixed feature types, prone to overfitting.   - Random Forests / Bagging: robust, good off-the-shelf performance, handle noisy features (e.g., bagged trees performed best in a prominent-syllable detection study).   - Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM): state-of-the-art for many tabular tasks; high performance with careful tuning.   - Support Vector Machines: effective for medium-sized datasets and margin-based problems; use kernels for nonlinearity.   - k-Nearest Neighbors: simple, nonparametric; expensive at prediction time and sensitive to scaling.   - Naive Bayes: fast, works well with high-dimensional sparse text features.   - Neural networks (DNNs, CNNs): best for large datasets, images, audio or when feature engineering is hard; heavier compute and tuning.   - Ensembles: combining models (bagging/boosting/stacks) often improves accuracy over single learners. Common pitfalls - Overfitting to training/validation due to excessive tuning or leakage. - Using accuracy on imbalanced datasets as the sole metric. - Ignoring data sampling bias or representativeness (e.g., remote-sensing sampling affects LULC classifier performance). - Failing to monitor model performance post-deployment.  Tools and libraries - scikit-learn (general classifiers, pipelines, CV), XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost (boosted trees), TensorFlow/PyTorch (neural nets), SHAP/LIME (explainability).  In short: choose models iteratively—baseline → stronger models → ensembles—guided by the data size, feature types, interpretability needs, and the right evaluation metrics; validate with robust cross-validation and watch for leakage and class imbalance.

Bottom line: start with a simple, interpretable baseline (e.g., logistic regression or single decision tree), evaluate with appropriate metrics and cross-validation, iterate with more powerful models (random forest, gradient boosting, or neural nets) only after careful feature work and validation, and guard against leakage and overfitting when deploying.
10|96:	Machine learning classifiers are supervised models that assign inputs to discrete categories. Practical guidance and a concise taxonomy:  What they are - Supervised algorithms trained on labeled examples to predict class labels for new data.  Common families (when to use) - Linear models (Logistic Regression, Linear SVM): fast, interpretable, good when classes are (roughly) linearly separable or as strong baselines. - Kernel SVMs: effective for smaller-to-moderate datasets with nonlinear boundaries. - Tree-based models (Decision Trees, Random Forests): handle mixed feature types, missing values, limited preprocessing; good default for tabular data. - Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost): state-of-the-art on many tabular problems—high accuracy with careful tuning. - k-Nearest Neighbors: simple, nonparametric; cost grows with data size. - Naive Bayes: fast and robust for high-dimensional, conditionally independent features (e.g., text). - Neural networks / deep learning: best for large datasets, images, audio, sequential data; require more data and tuning. - Ensembles (bagging, stacking): often improve robustness and accuracy by combining models.  Key practical steps 1. Start with a simple baseline (logistic regression or a single tree). 2. Preprocess: handle missing values, scale features if needed, encode categoricals, engineer informative features. 3. Address class imbalance (resampling, class weights, focal loss). 4. Use k-fold cross-validation and hold-out or external validation (multi-center validation when possible) to measure generalization. 5. Tune hyperparameters (grid/random search, Bayesian optimization) using validation folds. 6. Evaluate with appropriate metrics: accuracy, precision/recall, F1, ROC AUC, and Cohen’s kappa when class distributions/agreements matter. 7. Inspect model behavior and interpretability (feature importance, SHAP/LIME) before deployment. 8. Confirm robustness with external datasets and monitor post-deployment performance.  Selection rules of thumb - Prefer simple, interpretable models when data is small or decisions must be explainable. - Use tree ensembles or gradient boosting for best off-the-shelf performance on tabular data. - Use deep learning for large-scale, unstructured data (images, audio, text). - Try several algorithms—no single classifier is best for every problem (no free lunch).  Pitfalls to avoid - Overfitting through leakage or inadequate validation. - Relying solely on accuracy with imbalanced classes. - Ignoring domain knowledge and feature engineering.  In short: pick a simple baseline, validate carefully, iterate with tree ensembles or neural nets depending on data type and scale, and emphasize robust evaluation and interpretability before deployment.
1|91:	Below is a concise, practical Python scraper you can run locally. It:  - Lists files and subdirectories from the target directory page, - Optionally recurses into subdirectories, - Downloads files (streamed) to a local folder, - Uses polite defaults (custom User-Agent, delay, retries), - Avoids following parent-directory links ("..").  Important: check robots.txt and the site’s terms and ensure you have permission to download content before running this.  Script (Python 3.8+):  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import argparse import os import time import sys from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse, unquote import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup  HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "arcjav-scraper/1.0 (+https://example.local/)"} TIMEOUT = 15 RETRY_COUNT = 3  def safe_name_from_url(url):     path = unquote(urlparse(url).path)     name = os.path.basename(path.rstrip("/"))     if not name:         name = "index.html"     return name  def fetch_html(session, url):     for attempt in range(RETRY_COUNT):         try:             r = session.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=TIMEOUT)             r.raise_for_status()             return r.text         except Exception as e:             if attempt + 1 == RETRY_COUNT:                 raise             time.sleep(1 + attempt)     raise RuntimeError("unreachable")  def parse_links(html, base_url):     soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")     links = []     for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True):         href = a["href"]         # skip parent directory links         if href in ("../", ".."):             continue         full = urljoin(base_url, href)         links.append((full, a.get_text(strip=True)))     return links  def download_file(session, url, dest_path):     os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(dest_path), exist_ok=True)     # stream download     for attempt in range(RETRY_COUNT):         try:             with session.get(url, headers=HEADERS, stream=True, timeout=TIMEOUT) as r:                 r.raise_for_status()                 tmp = dest_path + ".part"                 with open(tmp, "wb") as f:                     for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):                         if chunk:                             f.write(chunk)                 os.replace(tmp, dest_path)                 return         except Exception as e:             if attempt + 1 == RETRY_COUNT:                 raise             time.sleep(1 + attempt)  def scrape_dir(session, url, out_dir, recursive=False, delay=0.5, visited=None):     if visited is None:         visited = set()     if url in visited:         return     visited.add(url)     print("Fetching directory:", url)     html = fetch_html(session, url)     links = parse_links(html, url)     for link, text in links:         # treat trailing slash as directory         if link.endswith("/"):             if recursive:                 subdir_name = safe_name_from_url(link)                 out_subdir = os.path.join(out_dir, subdir_name)                 scrape_dir(session, link, out_subdir, recursive, delay, visited)             else:                 print("Skipping subdirectory (use --recursive):", link)         else:             filename = safe_name_from_url(link)             out_path = os.path.join(out_dir, filename)             if os.path.exists(out_path):                 print("Exists, skipping:", filename)             else:                 print("Downloading:", filename)                 try:                     download_file(session, link, out_path)                 except Exception as e:                     print("Failed to download", link, "->", e, file=sys.stderr)             time.sleep(delay)  def main():     p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Simple directory scraper/downloader")     p.add_argument("url", help="Directory URL to scrape")     p.add_argument("-o", "--out", default="downloads", help="Output directory")     p.add_argument("-r", "--recursive", action="store_true", help="Recurse into subdirectories")     p.add_argument("-d", "--delay", type=float, default=0.5, help="Seconds between requests")     args = p.parse_args()      session = requests.Session()     try:         scrape_dir(session, args.url, args.out, recursive=args.recursive, delay=args.delay)     except Exception as e:         print("Error:", e, file=sys.stderr)         sys.exit(1)  if __name__ == "__main__":     main() ```  Run example: - Single directory listing: python scraper.py "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/" - Recursively: python scraper.py -r -o saved "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/"  If you want concurrency or more robust error handling, I can provide an asyncio/aiohttp version.

It respects robots.txt (checks before scraping), uses polite rate limiting, and is robust to URL encoding/Unicode.  Save as arcjav_scraper.py and run with Python 3.8+.  Code:  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ arcjav_scraper.py  Usage:     python arcjav_scraper.py "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/" \         --output items.json --delay 1.0  Notes:  - The script only reads the directory listing and produces metadata (name, url, is_dir).  - It checks robots.txt before scraping the target host.  - Be polite: set delay and a reasonable User-Agent. """ import argparse import json import time import urllib.parse import sys import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse  DEFAULT_UA = "arcjav-scraper/1.0 (+https://example.local/)"  def allowed_by_robots(target_url, user_agent=DEFAULT_UA):     parsed = urlparse(target_url)     robots_url = f"{parsed.scheme}://{parsed.netloc}/robots.txt"     try:         r = requests.get(robots_url, timeout=8, headers={"User-Agent": user_agent})         if r.status_code != 200:             return True  # no robots.txt => treat as allowed         # simple robots.txt parser: look for Disallow lines for our UA or '*'         rules = r.text.splitlines()         applicable = []         ua = None         for line in rules:             line = line.strip()             if not line or line.startswith('#'):                 continue             if line.lower().startswith("user-agent:"):                 ua = line.split(":", 1)[1].strip()                 applicable = []             elif line.lower().startswith("disallow:") and ua in (user_agent, "*", ""):                 path = line.split(":", 1)[1].strip()                 applicable.append(path)         # naive check: if any disallow is prefix of the path, block         path = parsed.path or "/"         for d in applicable:             if d == "":                 return True             if path.startswith(d):                 return False         return True     except Exception:         return True  # on error, be permissive (but you can change this)  def fetch_page(url, session, timeout=15):     r = session.get(url, timeout=timeout)     r.raise_for_status()     return r.text  def parse_directory_listing(html, base_url):     soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")     items = []     # Grab all anchor tags; directory listings normally use <a href="...">Name</a>     for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True):         href = a["href"].strip()         # skip up-directory links         if href in ("../", "/"):             continue         # build absolute URL         full = urljoin(base_url, href)         # Determine display name. Some listings put name in text, some in title attr         name = a.get_text(strip=True) or a.get("title") or href         # heuristics to detect directory: trailing slash or no extension         is_dir = href.endswith("/")         items.append({             "name": name,             "href": href,             "url": full,             "is_dir": is_dir         })     # Remove duplicates while preserving order     seen = set()     filtered = []     for it in items:         if it["url"] in seen:             continue         seen.add(it["url"])         filtered.append(it)     return filtered  def main():     p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Scrape a directory listing and output items as JSON.")     p.add_argument("url", help="Target directory URL")     p.add_argument("--output", "-o", default=None, help="Write JSON output to file (stdout if omitted)")     p.add_argument("--delay", type=float, default=0.8, help="Delay between requests (seconds)")     p.add_argument("--user-agent", default=DEFAULT_UA)     args = p.parse_args()      if not allowed_by_robots(args.url, user_agent=args.user_agent):         print("Robots.txt disallows scraping this path for the selected user-agent. Aborting.", file=sys.stderr)         sys.exit(1)      session = requests.Session()     session.headers.update({"User-Agent": args.user_agent, "Accept": "text/html,application/xhtml+xml"})      try:         html = fetch_page(args.url, session)     except Exception as e:         print(f"Error fetching page: {e}", file=sys.stderr)         sys.exit(1)      items = parse_directory_listing(html, args.url)      # Optionally: follow subdirectory entries (disabled by default)     # Example to recursively fetch one level deep:     # for it in list(items):     #     if it["is_dir"]:     #         time.sleep(args.delay)     #         try:     #             sub_html = fetch_page(it["url"], session)     #             subitems = parse_directory_listing(sub_html, it["url"])     #             it["children"] = subitems     #         except Exception as e:     #             it["children_error"] = str(e)      out = json.dumps({"source": args.url, "count": len(items), "items": items}, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)      if args.output:         with open(args.output, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:             f.write(out)         print(f"Wrote {len(items)} items to {args.output}")     else:         print(out)  if __name__ == "__main__":     main() ```  Quick notes and best practices - Always check robots.txt and the site terms (the script does a basic robots check). - Use conservative rate limits (delay) and a descriptive User-Agent. - This script collects metadata only. If you plan to download media files, ensure you have permission and add explicit checks and resumable downloads. - If the target uses JavaScript to render the listing, use a headless browser (Playwright/selenium) instead of requests/BS4.
3|91:	Here's a concise, ready-to-run Python scraper that lists links from that directory index and downloads the files it finds. It uses requests + BeautifulSoup, handles percent-encoded filenames, user-agent, simple retry and rate limiting. Before running, check the site’s robots.txt and terms and do not download copyrighted material you are not allowed to.  requirements: - Python 3.8+ - pip install requests beautifulsoup4  script (save as scrape_arcjav.py):  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os import time import argparse from urllib.parse import urljoin, unquote, urlparse import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup  HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "scraper-example/1.0 (+https://example.com)"}  def fetch_html(url, timeout=15):     r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=timeout)     r.raise_for_status()     return r.text  def parse_index(html, base_url):     soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")     links = []     for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True):         href = a["href"]         # skip parent dir links         if href in ("..", "../"):             continue         full = urljoin(base_url, href)         # treat entries that are not directories (no trailing slash) as files         if not href.endswith("/"):             # use basename of decoded path as filename             filename = os.path.basename(unquote(href))             if filename:                 links.append((filename, full))     return links  def download(url, out_path, chunk_size=8192, retries=2):     for attempt in range(retries + 1):         try:             with requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, stream=True, timeout=30) as r:                 r.raise_for_status()                 os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(out_path), exist_ok=True)                 with open(out_path, "wb") as f:                     for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size):                         if chunk:                             f.write(chunk)             return True         except Exception as e:             if attempt == retries:                 raise             time.sleep(2)     return False  def main():     parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Simple directory index scraper/downloader")     parser.add_argument("url", help="Index URL (e.g. the arcjav directory)")     parser.add_argument("-o", "--out", default="downloads", help="Output directory")     parser.add_argument("-d", "--delay", type=float, default=1.0, help="Delay between downloads (seconds)")     args = parser.parse_args()      index_html = fetch_html(args.url)     entries = parse_index(index_html, args.url)     if not entries:         print("No file links found on page.")         return      print(f"Found {len(entries)} files. Downloading to '{args.out}' (delay {args.delay}s).")     for i, (name, file_url) in enumerate(entries, 1):         safe_name = name.replace(os.path.sep, "_")         out_file = os.path.join(args.out, safe_name)         if os.path.exists(out_file):             print(f"[{i}/{len(entries)}] Skipping (exists): {safe_name}")             continue         try:             print(f"[{i}/{len(entries)}] Downloading: {safe_name}")             download(file_url, out_file)             time.sleep(args.delay)         except Exception as e:             print(f"[{i}/{len(entries)}] Failed {safe_name}: {e}")  if __name__ == "__main__":     main() ```  Usage example: - python scrape_arcjav.py "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/" -o ./album -d 0.8  Notes and troubleshooting: - If the server blocks simple requests (Cloudflare, worker protections), try increasing the User-Agent, adding reasonable headers, or use a headless browser (Playwright/Selenium). - If the listing contains subdirectories, adapt parse_index to follow directory links and recurse. - Respect rate limits, robots.txt and copyright; do not redistribute copyrighted material. Prerequisites: - Python 3.8+ - pip install requests beautifulsoup4 tqdm  Script (save as scrape_arc.py):  ``` #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os import time import logging from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser from tqdm import tqdm  logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format='%(levelname)s: %(message)s')  BASE_URL = "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/" USER_AGENT = "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; polite-scraper/1.0)" OUT_DIR = "downloaded_files" MAX_WORKERS = 4 REQUEST_DELAY = 0.5  # seconds between requests per worker RETRIES = 3 TIMEOUT = 20  session = requests.Session() session.headers.update({"User-Agent": USER_AGENT})  def ok_by_robots(url):     parsed = urlparse(url)     robots_url = f"{parsed.scheme}://{parsed.netloc}/robots.txt"     rp = RobotFileParser()     try:         rp.set_url(robots_url)         rp.read()         return rp.can_fetch(USER_AGENT, url)     except Exception:         # If robots.txt inaccessible, be conservative and allow (or change to False to be stricter)         logging.warning("Could not fetch robots.txt; proceeding but be careful.")         return True  def fetch_listing(url):     resp = session.get(url, timeout=TIMEOUT)     resp.raise_for_status()     soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, "html.parser")     links = []     for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True):         href = a["href"].strip()         # Skip parent directory link and query links         if href in ("../", "/") or href.startswith("?"):             continue         full = urljoin(url, href)         # Some directory listings include trailing slashes for dirs; here we only want files         if full.endswith("/"):             continue         links.append(full)     # dedupe while preserving order     seen = set()     out = []     for u in links:         if u not in seen:             seen.add(u)             out.append(u)     return out  def download_file(url, out_dir):     for attempt in range(1, RETRIES + 1):         try:             local_name = os.path.join(out_dir, os.path.basename(urlparse(url).path))             if os.path.exists(local_name) and os.path.getsize(local_name) > 0:                 logging.info("Already downloaded: %s", local_name)                 return local_name             with session.get(url, stream=True, timeout=TIMEOUT) as r:                 r.raise_for_status()                 os.makedirs(out_dir, exist_ok=True)                 total = int(r.headers.get("content-length", 0))                 with open(local_name + ".part", "wb") as f, tqdm(                     total=total, unit="B", unit_scale=True, desc=os.path.basename(local_name), leave=False                 ) as pbar:                     for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):                         if chunk:                             f.write(chunk)                             pbar.update(len(chunk))             os.replace(local_name + ".part", local_name)             # polite pause             time.sleep(REQUEST_DELAY)             return local_name         except Exception as e:             logging.warning("Attempt %d failed for %s: %s", attempt, url, e)             time.sleep(1 + attempt)     logging.error("Failed to download %s after %d attempts", url, RETRIES)     return None  def main():     url = BASE_URL     if not ok_by_robots(url):         logging.error("Blocked by robots.txt for URL: %s", url)         return     logging.info("Fetching listing: %s", url)     files = fetch_listing(url)     if not files:         logging.info("No files found at %s", url)         return     logging.info("Found %d files. Starting downloads to %s", len(files), OUT_DIR)      with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=MAX_WORKERS) as ex:         futures = {ex.submit(download_file, f, OUT_DIR): f for f in files}         for fut in as_completed(futures):             src = futures[fut]             try:                 res = fut.result()                 if res:                     logging.info("Downloaded: %s", res)                 else:                     logging.error("Failed: %s", src)             except Exception as e:                 logging.exception("Error for %s: %s", src, e)  if __name__ == "__main__":     main() ```  Notes and cautions: - Respect robots.txt, site terms of service and copyright law. Only download what you are allowed to. - If content is copyrighted or illegal, do not download or distribute it. - Reduce MAX_WORKERS and increase REQUEST_DELAY to be gentler on the server. - For large crawls, implement exponential backoff and persistent checkpointing. - If the listing is produced by JavaScript (dynamic), use a headless browser (Playwright/selenium) instead of requests. - If you need recursion into subfolders, modify fetch_listing to detect directories (href ending with "/") and recursively call it. Code (synchronous, easy to read)  ``` #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os import time import logging import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse, unquote import urllib.robotparser from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter, Retry from tqdm import tqdm  logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) session = requests.Session() retries = Retry(total=3, backoff_factor=0.8, status_forcelist=[429,500,502,503,504]) session.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retries)) session.headers.update({"User-Agent": "scraper/1.0 (+https://example.com)"})  def allowed_by_robots(target_url, user_agent="scraper/1.0"):     rp = urllib.robotparser.RobotFileParser()     parsed = urlparse(target_url)     robots_url = f"{parsed.scheme}://{parsed.netloc}/robots.txt"     try:         rp.set_url(robots_url)         rp.read()         return rp.can_fetch(user_agent, target_url)     except Exception:         # Code: ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import argparse import os import time from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse, unquote  import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from tqdm import tqdm  DEFAULT_USER_AGENT = "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; scraper/1.0; +https://example.com)"  def list_links(page_url, session):     r = session.get(page_url, timeout=30)     r.raise_for_status()     soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser")     links = []     for a in soup.select("a[href]"):         href = a["href"]         # Math (Lua): local function dot(a,b) return a.x*b.x + a.y*b.y + a.z*b.z end local function reflect(v, n)     local d = 2 * dot(v, n)     return v - n * d end  Server-side physics loop (pseudo-Lua): local ball = {pos = vector3(x,y,z), vel = vector3(0,0,0), radius = 0.18} local gravity = vector3(0,0,-9.81) local dt = 0.02 local restitution = 0.65 local friction = 0.8  Citizen.CreateThread(function()     while true do         Wait(math.floor(dt*1000))         -- integrate         ball.vel = ball.vel + gravity * dt         ball.pos = ball.pos + ball.vel * dt          -- ground check via raycast down from ball.pos         local ray = StartShapeTestRay(ball.pos.x, ball.pos.y, ball.pos.z, ball.pos.x, ball.pos.y, ball.pos.z - 5|94:	Short version: run the ball’s physics on whoever owns the entity, raycast each tick from the ball’s previous to current position to detect hits (GetShapeTestResult), compute a reflected velocity using the hit normal and a restitution coefficient, then SetEntityVelocity/ApplyForceToEntity. For player “hits”, detect contact (IsEntityTouchingEntity or a short shape test from the player’s hand/foot) and add an impulse based on the player’s forward vector + upward component. Always ensure network control before changing velocity so other clients see it.  Example implementation (client or server script that has control of the ball):  1) Per-tick collision + bounce (pseudo-Lua) local restitution = 0.75 -- bounce strength (0..1) local friction = 0.98    -- planar friction on bounce local prevPos = GetEntityCoords(ball)  Citizen.CreateThread(function()   while DoesEntityExist(ball) do     Citizen.Wait(0)     local pos = GetEntityCoords(ball)     -- raycast from previous to current to catch fast movement     local ray = StartShapeTestRay(prevPos.x, prevPos.y, prevPos.z, pos.x, pos.y, pos.z, -1, ball, 7)     local _, hit, hitCoords, hitNormal, hitEntity = GetShapeTestResult(ray)     if hit then       -- retrieve current velocity       local vx, vy, vz = table.unpack(GetEntityVelocity(ball))       local v = {x=vx, y=vy, z=vz}       -- reflect v about normal: v' = v - 2*(v·n)*n       local dot = v.x*hitNormal.x + v.y*hitNormal.y + v.z*hitNormal.z       local rvx = v.x - 2*dot*hitNormal.x       local rvy = v.y - 2*dot*hitNormal.y       local rvz = v.z - 2*dot*hitNormal.z       -- apply restitution + friction on horizontal plane       rvx = rvx * restitution * friction       rvy = rvy * restitution * friction       rvz = rvz * restitution       -- nudge ball out of surface to avoid sticking       local pushout = 0.03       SetEntityCoordsNoOffset(ball, hitCoords.x + hitNormal.x*pushout, hitCoords.y + hitNormal.y*pushout, hitCoords.z + hitNormal.z*pushout, false, false, false)       SetEntityVelocity(ball, rvx, rvy, rvz)     end     prevPos = pos   end end)  2) Player hit / impulse -- when you detect player contacting the ball (collision, IsEntityTouchingEntity, or a small capsule/ray from hand) local function applyPlayerHit(ball, playerPed)   -- get directions & velocity   local px, py, pz = table.unpack(GetEntityCoords(playerPed))   local forward = GetEntityForwardVector(playerPed) -- returns vector3   local playerVelX, playerVelY, playerVelZ = table.unpack(GetEntityVelocity(playerPed))   -- tune these   local forwardPower = 8.0   local upPower = 3.5   local influence = 0.5 -- add some of player velocity to ball   -- compute impulse   local impX = forward.x * forwardPower + 0.0   local impY = forward.y * forwardPower + 0.0   local impZ = forward.z * forwardPower + upPower   impX = impX + playerVelX * influence   impY = impY + playerVelY * influence   impZ = impZ + playerVelZ * influence   -- add to current velocity (or set directly)   local bvx, bvy, bvz = table.unpack(GetEntityVelocity(ball))   SetEntityVelocity(ball, bvx + impX, bvy + impY, bvz + impZ) end  3) Network considerations - Make the ball a networked entity and ensure one script instance is authoritative (typically server or host). Before manipulating physics call NetworkRequestControlOfEntity(ball) and check NetworkHasControlOfEntity(ball). - If authority changes frequently, you must replicate position/velocity to avoid jitter. Prefer server-authoritative simulation for fairness. - Use SetEntityDynamic(ball, true) / SetEntityCollision to ensure natural collisions work.  Tuning tips - Use smaller physics timestep (Wait(0)) for stability. - Tune restitution (0–1) and friction for realistic bounces. - Use shape tests rather than only HasEntityCollidedWithAnything for stable hits at high speeds. - To detect "ground" specifically, check hitNormal nearly (0,0,1) or hitEntity == 0 / check material via GetEntitySurfaceType (if available) — otherwise treat any hit where hitNormal.z > 0.6 as ground. 9|94:	Short answer: treat the ball as a dynamic entity, detect collisions each tick with either a capsule shape test (robust) or a ground-Z check (simple), and when you detect a hit compute a physics response by reflecting/applying an impulse to the ball using the collision normal or the player's hit vector. Below are the key ideas and a compact example you can adapt.  Key points - Create the ball as a dynamic/world object (CreateObject), enable collisions and physics (SetEntityCollision, SetEntityDynamic). - Detect collisions:   - Robust: StartShapeTestCapsule between lastPos and currPos with the ball radius → GetShapeTestResult returns hit + surface normal and hit entity.   - Simple: GetGroundZFor3dCoord or compare ball z to groundZ + radius to detect ground contact only. - Compute response:   - For world/ground bounce: reflect current velocity about the hit normal: v' = v - 2*(v·n)*n and multiply by a restitution (0..1).   - For player hits: compute hit direction from the player (hand bone or forward/aim vector), form an impulse vector and ApplyForceToEntity or SetEntityVelocity. - Sync: physics run client-side are smoother but you’ll need server-side authority or periodic network sync (NetworkGetNetworkIdFromEntity / SetNetworkIdExistsOnAllMachines) for multiplayer consistency.  Compact example (client-side, adapt names/IDs and networking as needed)  ```lua -- helpers local function vecsub(a,b) return {x=a.x-b.x,y=a.y-b.y,z=a.z-b.z} end local function vecadd(a,b) return {x=a.x+b.x,y=a.y+b.y,z=a.z+b.z} end local function vecmul(a,s) return {x=a.x*s,y=a.y*s,z=a.z*s} end local function vecdot(a,b) return a.x*b.x + a.y*b.y + a.z*b.z end local function veclen(a) return math.sqrt(vecdot(a,a)) end local function vecnorm(a) local L=veclen(a) if L==0 then return {x=0,y=0,z=0} end return vecmul(a,1/L) end  local ball = CreateObject(GetHashKey("prop_beach_volleyball_01"), x,y,z, true, true, true) SetEntityCollision(ball, true, true) SetEntityDynamic(ball, true) local radius = 0.35 local restitution = 0.75  local lastPos = GetEntityCoords(ball)  Citizen.CreateThread(function()   while true do     Citizen.Wait(0)     local pos = GetEntityCoords(ball)     -- Robust capsule test between lastPos and pos     local handle = StartShapeTestCapsule(lastPos.x,lastPos.y,lastPos.z, pos.x,pos.y,pos.z, radius, 10, ball, 7)     local _, hit, hitCoord, hitNormal, hitEnt = GetShapeTestResult(handle)     if hit then       -- world ground or object collision       local vel = GetEntityVelocity(ball)       local v = {x=vel.x,y=vel.y,z=vel.z}       local n = {x=hitNormal.x,y=hitNormal.y,z=hitNormal.z}       local dot = vecdot(v,n)       local reflect = vecsub(v, vecmul(n, 2*dot))       reflect = vecmul(reflect, restitution)       -- set new velocity (instant bounce)       SetEntityVelocity(ball, reflect.x, reflect.y, reflect.z)       -- optional: nudge ball slightly out of collision to avoid stuck       SetEntityCoords(ball, hitCoord.x + n.x* (radius+0.01), hitCoord.y + n.y*(radius+0.01), hitCoord.z + n.z*(radius+0.01), false, false, false, true)     end      -- player hit check (example: press E to hit when close)     local playerPed = PlayerPedId()     local playerPos = GetEntityCoords(playerPed)     local dist = #(vector3(pos.x,pos.y,pos.z) - playerPos) -- shorthand: calculate distance     if IsControlJustPressed(0, 38) and dist < 2.0 then -- E key       -- get hit direction from player's forward or hand bone       local forw = GetEntityForwardVector(playerPed)       local aimUp = 0.6 -- tune upward component       local power = 12.0 -- tune power       local dir = vecnorm({x=forw.x, y=forw.y, z=forw.z + aimUp})       local impulse = vecmul(dir, power)       -- apply instantaneous velocity or force       SetEntityVelocity(ball, impulse.x, impulse.y, impulse.z)       -- or ApplyForceToEntity(ball, 1, impulse.x, impulse.y, impulse.z, 0,0,0, 1, false, true, true, false, true)     end      lastPos = pos   end end) ```  Tuning and notes - Tune radius, restitution, hit power and upward component to get the desired arcade feel. - StartShapeTestCapsule is best to catch fast-moving balls; for very high speed, sweep test with larger steps or substep the simulation. - For realistic spin, add angular velocity: Use SetEntityAngularVelocity if available or ApplyForce at offset to create torque. - Networking: choose authoritative model. Either run physics on the server and broadcast positions (heavy), or run client-side physics and periodically correct via server to avoid desync. - Performance: do most heavy math only when ball moved significantly; lower tick rate if necessary.  This approach gives deterministic, tuneable volleyball behavior: capsule tests for collision detection, reflection for bounces, and player impulses for volleys.

Code:  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import time import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse  START_URL = "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/"  session = requests.Session() session.headers.update({"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (crawler)"})  seen_dirs = set() files = set()  def is_directory_link(href):     # treat links ending with '/' as directories     return href.endswith('/')  def crawl_dir(url):     if url in seen_dirs:         return     seen_dirs.add(url)     try:         r = session.get(url, timeout=15)         r.raise_for_status()     except Exception as e:         print("Failed to fetch", url, ":", e)         return      soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser")     for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True):         href = a["href"].strip()         # skip parent links, query-only links, anchors         if href in ("../", "/", "") or href.startswith("?") or href.startswith("#"):             continue          full = urljoin(url, href)         # avoid jumping to other hosts         if urlparse(full).netloc != urlparse(START_URL).netloc:             continue          if is_directory_link(href) or full.endswith('/'):             crawl_dir(full)             time.sleep(0.15)  # polite delay         else:             files.add(full)  if __name__ == "__main__":     crawl_dir(START_URL)     with open("files.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:         for u in sorted(files):             f.write(u + "\n")     print(f"Found {len(files)} files. Written to files.txt") ```  Notes: - If the listing is rendered by JavaScript, this simple HTML parser won't see subdirectory links; in that case use a headless browser (selenium/playwright) to render pages first. - Adjust the polite delay (time.sleep) if you need faster or slower crawling. - This assumes the directory index uses normal <a href="..."> links (typical Apache/nginx/Workers directory listings).
6|98:	Use a small Python crawler that follows directory links and collects all non-directory links. This example uses requests + BeautifulSoup and urljoin to normalize links. Run only on servers you have permission to crawl and respect robots.txt and copyright law.  Requirements: - pip install requests beautifulsoup4  Script:  ```python import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse  def list_files(root_url, session=None):     if session is None:         session = requests.Session()     visited = set()     stack = [root_url]     files = []      while stack:         url = stack.pop()         if url in visited:             continue         visited.add(url)          resp = session.get(url, timeout=30)         resp.raise_for_status()         soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, "html.parser")          for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True):             href = a["href"].strip()             if href in ("../", "/", ""):                 continue             full = urljoin(url, href)             # normalize (drop fragments)             p = urlparse(full)             full = p._replace(fragment="").geturl()              # Heuristic: links ending with / are directories; others are files.             if full.endswith("/"):                 if full not in visited:                     stack.append(full)             else:                 files.append(full)      return files  if __name__ == "__main__":     root = "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/"     all_files = list_files(root)     for f in all_files:         print(f) ```  Notes: - This uses a simple heuristic (trailing slash) to detect directories; if the server doesn't include trailing slashes you can do a HEAD request and treat responses with Content-Type "text/html" as directories and others as files. - Be mindful of rate limits; add delays if needed.

Example Python 3 script (requires requests and beautifulsoup4):  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # pip install requests beautifulsoup4  import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse import sys  base = "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/" if not base.endswith("/"):     base += "/"  seen = set() files = set()  def crawl(url):     if url in seen:         return     seen.add(url)     try:         r = requests.get(url, timeout=15)         r.raise_for_status()     except Exception as e:         # skip unreachable pages         return     soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser")     for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True):         href = a["href"].strip()         # ignore parent links and anchors/queries         if href in ("../", "..") or href.startswith("#") or href.startswith("mailto:") or href.startswith("?"):             continue         full = urljoin(url, href)         # stay under the base path only         if not full.startswith(base):             continue         # directories typically end with '/'         if href.endswith("/"):             crawl(full)         else:             files.add(full)  if __name__ == "__main__":     crawl(base)     for f in sorted(files):         print(f) ```  Usage: - Save as list_urls.py and run python3 list_urls.py > urls.txt  Notes: - This assumes the server’s directory listing uses anchor tags (typical Apache/Nginx listings). 8|98:	Save and run this Python script. It recursively crawls the given directory index page, follows subdirectory links (hrefs that end with "/") and prints all file URLs it finds. Requires requests and beautifulsoup4 (pip install requests beautifulsoup4).  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import sys import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse, urlunparse  HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (file-list-crawler)"}  def normalize(url):     p = urlparse(url)     # drop query and fragment for consistency     return urlunparse((p.scheme, p.netloc, p.path, "", "", ""))  def crawl(base_url):     base_url = normalize(base_url)     parsed_base = urlparse(base_url)     seen = set()     files = []      session = requests.Session()     session.headers.update(HEADERS)      def visit(url):         url = normalize(url)         if url in seen:             return         seen.add(url)          try:             r = session.get(url, timeout=15)             r.raise_for_status()         except Exception as e:             # skip pages we can't fetch             return          soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser")         for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True):             href = a["href"].strip()             # skip parent, anchors and query-only links             if href in ("../", "/", "#") or href.startswith("?") or href.startswith("#"):                 continue             full = urljoin(url, href)             full = normalize(full)              # keep only links within the same host/path prefix             p = urlparse(full)             if p.netloc != parsed_base.netloc:                 continue             if not p.path.startswith(parsed_base.path):                 continue              # directories usually end with '/'             if href.endswith("/"):                 visit(full)             else:                 files.append(full)      visit(base_url)     return files  if __name__ == "__main__":     if len(sys.argv) > 1:         start = sys.argv[1]     else:         start = "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/"     for f in crawl(start):         print(f) ```  Run: python3 list_files.py or python3 list_files.py "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/"
9|98:	Below is a small Python crawler that recursively parses the directory index pages and collects direct file URLs. It uses requests + BeautifulSoup and only follows links inside the starting folder.  Requirements: - Python 3 - pip install requests beautifulsoup4  Code:  ```python import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse import sys  def crawl_dir(start_url):     if not start_url.endswith('/'):         start_url += '/'     seen = set()     files = []      def crawl(url):         if url in seen:             return         seen.add(url)         try:             r = requests.get(url, timeout=10)             r.raise_for_status()         except Exception as e:             print(f"skip {url} ({e})", file=sys.stderr)             return          # If this page is not HTML, treat it as a file (rare for directory listing root)         ctype = r.headers.get('Content-Type', '')         if 'text/html' not in ctype:             files.append(url)             return          soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')         for a in soup.find_all('a', href=True):             href = a['href'].strip()             # skip parent/sorting anchors and fragments             if href.startswith('?') or href.startswith('#') or href in ('../', '/'):                 continue             full = urljoin(url, href)             # only follow links inside the starting folder             if not full.startswith(start_url):                 continue             # skip obvious parent directory text links             if a.text.strip() in ('Parent Directory', '..'):                 continue             if href.endswith('/'):                 crawl(full)             else:                 # final file URL                 files.append(full)      crawl(start_url)     # remove duplicates while preserving order     seen_files = []     seen_f = set()     for f in files:         if f not in seen_f:             seen_files.append(f)             seen_f.add(f)     return seen_files  if __name__ == '__main__':     start = "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/"     file_urls = crawl_dir(start)     for u in file_urls:         print(u) ```  Notes: - This assumes the directory pages are HTML directory indexes with <a href="..."> for files and subfolders (typical for HTTP file listings). - If the server returns non-HTML for directories or blocks crawling, you may need to use HEAD requests or a different approach (or add retries/headers).
10|98:	Here's a simple, practical Python script that recursively crawls an HTML directory listing and prints (and optionally saves) all direct file URLs under the given base URL. It uses requests + BeautifulSoup, follows only same-root links, avoids parent links, and does a small delay to be polite.  Save as list_files.py and run with Python 3.  Code: ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup from urllib.parse import urljoin, urlparse import time  HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "listing-bot/1.0 (+https://example.com)"} SLEEP = 0.2  # polite delay between requests  def is_same_root(url, root):     return urlparse(url).netloc == urlparse(root).netloc and url.startswith(root)  def collect_file_urls(start_url, max_pages=1000):     visited = set()     file_urls = set()     stack = [start_url]     root = start_url if start_url.endswith('/') else start_url + '/'      while stack and len(visited) < max_pages:         url = stack.pop()         if url in visited:             continue         visited.add(url)         try:             resp = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=15)         except Exception:             continue         time.sleep(SLEEP)          # if the response is not HTML treat it as a file         ctype = resp.headers.get("Content-Type", "")         if "text/html" not in ctype:             file_urls.add(url)             continue          soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, "html.parser")         for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True):             href = a["href"].split("#", 1)[0]  # drop fragment             if href in ("", "/", "../"):                 continue             # build absolute URL             child = urljoin(url, href)             # normalize trailing slash for directory detection             if not child.startswith(root):                 continue             # skip upward navigation             if ".." in child and child.rstrip("/").endswith(".."):                 continue              # heuristics: href ending with '/' -> directory; else assume file,             # but if file looks like HTML page we will fetch and check content-type on that iteration             if href.endswith("/"):                 if child not in visited:                     stack.append(child)             else:                 # push file candidate; if it's actually HTML (directory) we'll fetch and recurse later                 if child not in visited:                     stack.append(child)      # Anything remaining in visited that was fetched with non-HTML was added to file_urls;     # Some file candidates might still be HTML pages (index files) and will be included here if not filtered.     return sorted(file_urls)  if __name__ == "__main__":     base = "https://arcjav.arcjavdb.workers.dev/0:/001-050/%E4%B8%8A%E5%8E%9F%E4%BA%9A%E8%A1%A3/"     files = collect_file_urls(base)     # print to console     for f in files:         print(f)     # optionally write to file:     with open("file_urls.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as out:         for f in files:             out.write(f + "\n") ```  Notes and tips - Adjust SLEEP and max_pages to avoid overloading the host. - If the server doesn't set Content-Type for files, the script still treats non-HTML responses as files. If directory listings don't put trailing slashes on folder links, increase robustness by doing a HEAD request and checking Content-Type before deciding to recurse. - If you prefer a one-liner, wget can also spider a directory: wget --spider -r -np -nd URL and parse its output, but the Python approach gives more control.

1|93:	Below is a concise, textbook-style summary of the anatomy (location), arterial and venous supply, innervation, histology and primary physiology for the parts of the renal/urinary system: kidney (whole organ and nephron components), calyces/pelvis, ureter, urinary bladder and urethra.  1) Kidney (organ) - Location/anatomy: Paired retroperitoneal organs at T12–L3 level; right slightly lower. Medial hilum transmits renal artery, vein and ureter. Internally: cortex (outer), medulla (renal pyramids with papillae), minor/major calyces and renal pelvis. - Arteries/veins: Renal artery from abdominal aorta → anterior and posterior divisions → 5 segmental arteries (end arteries) → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular → afferent arterioles. Venous return: interlobular → arcuate → interlobar → renal vein → IVC. Left renal vein is longer and commonly receives left gonadal and left suprarenal veins. - Nerves: Renal (periarterial) plexus—predominantly sympathetic fibers from thoracic/upper lumbar splanchnic/hypogastric plexuses; parasympathetic input is limited/variable. Sympathetic nerves modulate renal blood flow, tubular function and renin release. - Histology (gross/microscopic): Cortex contains renal corpuscles (glomeruli + Bowman’s capsule) and proximal/distal tubules; medulla contains loops of Henle and collecting ducts arranged in pyramids. Renal corpuscle: parietal layer (simple squamous), visceral layer of podocytes; proximal tubule: cuboidal epithelium with prominent brush border; thin limbs: squamous; thick ascending limb and distal convoluted tubule: cuboidal, less brush border; collecting duct: columnar epithelium with principal and intercalated cells. Vascular elements (glomerular capillaries, peritubular capillaries, vasa recta). - Physiology (organ-level & major functions): Filtration of plasma in glomeruli (GFR determined by hydrostatic/oncotic pressures and arteriolar tone); selective reabsorption and secretion along tubules; concentration of urine via countercurrent multiplication and vasa recta countercurrent exchange; regulation of blood volume/pressure (salt/water handling, renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system), acid–base balance, erythropoietin production, calcitriol (1,25‑OH2 vitamin D) activation, excretion of metabolic wastes and xenobiotics.  2) Nephron (functional unit) — key segments and functions - Renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman’s space): filtration barrier (fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, podocyte slit diaphragms); produces primary filtrate. - Proximal convoluted tubule: bulk reabsorption of Na+, water, glucose, amino acids; secretion of organic anions/cations. - Loop of Henle: thin descending limb—permeable to water; thin/thick ascending limb—impermeable to water, active NaCl reabsorption (diluting segment). - Distal convoluted tubule: fine-tuning of Na+, Ca2+ handling (PTH-sensitive), variable water permeability under ADH influence downstream. - Collecting duct (including cortical, medullary collecting ducts): final adjustment of water and urea; ADH-regulated water reabsorption; site for acid–base regulation (intercalated cells).  3) Minor/major calyces and renal pelvis - Location/anatomy: papillae drain into minor calyces → major calyces → renal pelvis → ureter. - Arteries/veins: small branches derived from adjacent renal arterial/venous branches; no separate named major vessels. - Nerves: branches of renal/ureteric plexuses. - Histology: mucosa lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium) over lamina propria; muscular coat continuous with ureter. - Physiology: passive conduit and initial peristaltic propulsion of urine into ureter; transitional epithelium protects against urine.  4) Ureter - Location/anatomy: muscular tube ~25–30 cm from renal pelvis to bladder, retroperitoneal; three natural constrictions (pelvi‑ureteric junction, pelvic brim crossing, ureterovesical junction). - Arteries/veins: blood supply segmental—renal, gonadal, common iliac/ureteric branches, superior and inferior vesical arteries; venous drainage parallels arteries to renal/gonadal/iliac veins. - Nerves: sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers from renal, aortic, and hypogastric plexuses; visceral sensory fibers convey pain (referred to T11–L2 dermatomes for upper ureter, S2–S4 for pelvic ureter). - Histology: mucosa—transitional epithelium; muscularis—inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle (distal third gains extra outer longitudinal layer); adventitia. - Physiology: peristaltic waves generated by pacemaker cells in pelvis propel urine; peristalsis amplitude and frequency modulated by autonomic input and local stretch.  5) Urinary bladder - Location/anatomy: midline pelvic organ (in pelvis when empty; rises into abdomen when full). Trigone demarcated by ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice. - Arteries/veins: superior and inferior vesical arteries (male); superior vesical and vaginal or inferior vesical branches in female; venous plexus drains to internal iliac veins. - Nerves: parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) cause detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation; sympathetic hypogastric (T11–L2) mediate bladder relaxation and internal sphincter contraction; somatic pudendal (S2–S4) controls external urethral sphincter (voluntary). - Histology: mucosa—transitional epithelium with rugae; submucosa; muscularis (detrusor) layers of smooth muscle in multiple orientations; adventitia/serosa on superior surface. - Physiology: urine storage (detrusor relaxed, sphincters closed) and coordinated micturition reflex—parasympathetic activation causes detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation; voluntary control via external sphincter.  6) Urethra - Location/anatomy: conduit from bladder to exterior. Female: short (~4 cm), opens anterior to vagina. Male: longer (~20 cm), divided into prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts. - Arteries/veins: branches of internal pudendal and inferior vesical/vaginal arteries; venous drainage to internal pudendal/internal iliac veins. - Nerves: somatic pudendal (external sphincter control), autonomic fibers supply mucosal vasculature and glands. - Histology: transitional epithelium in prostatic urethra → pseudostratified/stratified columnar in membranous/penile urethra → stratified squamous near external meatus; urethral glands in male. - Physiology: final conduit for urine/ejaculate; sphincter mechanisms (internal—autonomic; external—somatic) maintain continence.  Clinical/physiologic notes emphasized in textbooks - Renal arteries are end-arteries: segmental branch occlusion causes segmental ischemia/infraction. - Two nephron classes: cortical (short loops) and juxtamedullary (long loops important for urine concentration). - Autonomic control: renal sympathetic activity reduces renal blood flow and increases renin release; pelvic splanchnics are essential for bladder emptying. - Transitional epithelium throughout collecting system tolerates stretch and urine exposure.
