2|93:	Below is a concise, textbook-style summary of the renal (urinary) system broken into its main parts (kidneys, collecting system/renal pelvis & calyces, ureters, bladder, urethra). For each part I state: location/anatomy, arterial/venous/nerve supply, key histology, and principal physiology.  1) Kidneys - Location/anatomy: Paired retroperitoneal organs at roughly T12–L3. Right kidney lies slightly lower than left (liver). Hilum on medial border conveys renal artery, vein, lymphatics and ureter. Internal: cortex, medulla (medullary pyramids), papillae, minor/major calyces, renal pelvis. - Arteries/veins/nerves:   - Arteries: renal arteries from abdominal aorta → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular → afferent arterioles. Accessory/aberrant renal arteries common.   - Veins: interlobular → arcuate → interlobar → renal vein → inferior vena cava (renal vein exits anterior to artery).   - Nerves: renal plexus (predominantly sympathetic fibers from lower thoracic/upper lumbar splanchnic nerves via aorticorenal/celiac plexuses); parasympathetic input is minor (vagal fibers reported). - Histology:   - Cortex: renal corpuscles (glomeruli + Bowman's capsules), proximal and distal convoluted tubules.   - Medulla: straight tubules (loops of Henle), collecting ducts arranged into pyramids; vasa recta in medulla.   - Capsule: fibrous capsule with perirenal fat externally. - Physiology:   - Filtration at glomeruli (formation of primary filtrate).   - Tubular reabsorption and secretion along PCT, loop of Henle (countercurrent multiplier), DCT, collecting duct (ADH/aldosterone responsive).   - Concentration of urine via countercurrent exchange (vasa recta + loop of Henle).   - Endocrine roles: renin secretion (JG apparatus) → RAAS, erythropoietin production, activation of vitamin D (1α-hydroxylation).  2) Minor calyces, major calyces, renal pelvis (collecting system) - Location/anatomy: Minor calyces receive papillary urine; several merge to major calyces → renal pelvis, which narrows to form ureter at hilum. - Arteries/veins/nerves: supplied/drained by branches that supply the kidney (small branches from renal arteries/veins); innervation via renal and ureteric plexuses. - Histology: transitional epithelium (urothelium) lining with lamina propria; muscular coat where pelvis transitions to ureter. - Physiology: passive collection funneling urine from papillae into ureter; minimal absorptive role.  3) Ureters - Location/anatomy: Muscular tubes ~25–30 cm from renal pelvis to posterolateral bladder wall. Retroperitoneal along abdomen, cross pelvic brim near bifurcation of common iliac arteries, enter bladder obliquely (helps prevent reflux). - Arteries/veins/nerves:   - Arteries: upper ureter from renal artery branches; middle from gonadal/common iliac branches; lower from branches of internal iliac (e.g., vesical arteries).   - Veins: drain to renal, gonadal, and internal iliac venous systems accordingly.   - Nerves: sympathetic (T10–L2 via renal, aortic, and hypogastric plexuses) and parasympathetic (proximal contribution from vagus is minimal; distal ureter receives pelvic splanchnic S2–S4). Sensory fibers follow sympathetic pathways (referred pain to flank/groin). - Histology: lumen lined by transitional epithelium; lamina propria and well-developed muscularis (inner longitudinal + outer circular; distal ureter develops an outer longitudinal layer). - Physiology: peristaltic waves (pacemaker activity in renal pelvis/upper ureter + autonomic modulation) propel urine to bladder; anti-reflux mechanism at vesicoureteric junction.  4) Urinary bladder - Location/anatomy: Subperitoneal hollow muscular organ in pelvis. In males rests on prostate; in females rests on anterior vaginal wall and uterus. When empty lies in lesser pelvis; when full rises into abdomen. - Arteries/veins/nerves:   - Arteries: superior vesical arteries (from umbilical/internal iliac), inferior vesical artery (male) or vaginal artery (female) for inferior bladder.   - Veins: vesical venous plexus → internal iliac veins.   - Nerves: pelvic plexus: parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) cause detrusor contraction and relaxation of internal sphincter during voiding; sympathetic hypogastric nerves (T10–L2) promote storage (detrusor relaxation and internal sphincter contraction); somatic pudendal nerve (S2–S4) controls external urethral sphincter. - Histology: mucosa of transitional epithelium (urothelium) over lamina propria; muscularis (detrusor) composed of interlacing smooth muscle bundles (three poorly defined layers); serosa/peritoneum superiorly. - Physiology: reservoir with high compliance; storage phase mediated by sympathetic/somatic pathways; micturition reflex integrated in sacral spinal cord and brainstem (parasympathetic triggered contraction + somatic inhibition for voluntary voiding).  5) Urethra - Location/anatomy: conduit from bladder to exterior. Male urethra ~18–20 cm (prostatic, membranous, spongy/penile segments); female urethra ~3–4 cm, opens anterior to vaginal vestibule. - Arteries/veins/nerves:   - Arteries: branches from internal pudendal and vesical/vaginal arteries.   - Veins: drain to internal pudendal/internal iliac systems.   - Nerves: somatic pudendal (external sphincter control), autonomic components modulate urethral glands and internal sphincter (male). - Histology: proximate mucosal lining varies: transitional near bladder → pseudostratified columnar → stratified squamous near external meatus (male sequence varies by segment; female urethra predominantly transitional to stratified squamous). Lamina propria and muscular layer present. - Physiology: final conduit for urine elimination; sphincteric control: internal sphincter (smooth muscle, autonomic) and external sphincter (striated muscle, voluntary via pudendal).  Key integrated points (textbook emphasis) - Renal arterial branches are end-arteries (segmental arteries do not anastomose significantly); occlusion causes segmental ischemia. - Countercurrent multiplier (loop of Henle) and countercurrent exchanger (vasa recta) are central to urine concentration. - Autonomic control balances storage (sympathetic + somatic) versus voiding (parasympathetic + somatic inhibition) under spinal and supraspinal regulation. - Transitional epithelium (urothelium) lines collecting system, ureters, bladder and proximal urethra — specialized to stretch and form a urine-tight barrier. 3|93:	Below is a concise, textbook-style summary of anatomy (location and relations), arterial/venous/lymphatic/nerve supply, histology, and main physiological function for each principal part of the renal (urinary) system: kidney, calyces/renal pelvis, ureter, urinary bladder, and urethra.  1) Kidney - Location & gross anatomy   - Retroperitoneal, T12–L3 (right a little lower). Bean-shaped; convex lateral and concave medial border with renal hilum (renal artery, vein, ureter).   - Internal: cortex (outer), medulla (inner) organized into renal pyramids; pyramid apex = renal papilla draining into minor calyx. Cortex contains cortical labyrinth and cortical columns (of Bertin). - Arterial supply   - Renal artery (from aorta) → segmental arteries (end arteries, no significant anastomoses) → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular → afferent arterioles → glomerular capillaries.   - Accessory/aberrant renal arteries common. - Venous drainage   - Peritubular capillaries/vasa recta → interlobular veins → arcuate → interlobar → renal vein → IVC (left renal vein longer, crosses anterior to aorta). - Lymphatics   - Drain to lateral (para‑aortic) lymph nodes. - Nerves   - Renal plexus: primarily sympathetic (preganglionic from thoracic splanchnic nerves to aorticorenal ganglia), some sensory; parasympathetic input is limited/variable (vagal fibers described but minor). Sympathetic modulates renal blood flow, renin release. - Histology (nephron & collecting system)   - Nephron types: cortical (short loops) and juxtamedullary (long loops, vasa recta).   - Glomerulus: capillary tuft with fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane, visceral epithelial cells (podocytes), and Bowman’s (parietal) capsule.   - Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): simple cuboidal epithelium with dense brush border (microvilli) — major site of reabsorption.   - Loop of Henle: thin segments (simple squamous) and thick ascending limb (simple cuboidal/low columnar, no brush border).   - Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): simple cuboidal, fewer microvilli.   - Collecting ducts: simple cuboidal to columnar epithelium; principal and intercalated cells (acid–base handling).   - Juxtaglomerular apparatus: macula densa (DCT cells) + juxtaglomerular (granular) cells (renin secretion). - Physiology (key functions)   - Filtration of plasma at glomerulus; selective reabsorption and secretion along tubules; concentration of urine via countercurrent multiplier (loop of Henle) and vasa recta.   - Regulation of volume, electrolytes (Na+, K+, H+, HCO3–), acid–base balance.   - Endocrine roles: renin (RAAS), erythropoietin (EPO), activation of vitamin D (1α‑hydroxylase).  2) Minor calyces, major calyces and renal pelvis - Location & gross anatomy   - Minor calyx collects urine from a single papilla; several minor calyces form a major calyx; major calyces converge to form the renal pelvis within the renal sinus, which continues as the ureter. - Arterial/venous/lymphatics/nerves   - Vascular supply from small branches of renal artery/segmental branches; venous drainage to renal vein. Lymphatics to para‑aortic nodes. Innervation predominantly sympathetic and visceral sensory from renal/ureteric plexuses. - Histology   - Lined by transitional (urothelium) epithelium; lamina propria of connective tissue; muscular coat is sparse in calyces and increases in pelvis (smooth muscle arranged circumferentially/longitudinally). - Physiology   - Passive conduit and reservoir for urine from papillae to ureter; pelvic smooth muscle contributes to coordinated urine propulsion into the ureter.  3) Ureter - Location & gross anatomy   - Muscular tube (~25–30 cm) retroperitoneal from renal pelvis (L1) to posterior bladder wall. Three constrictions: ureteropelvic junction, where crosses pelvic brim/iliac vessels, and ureterovesical junction. - Arterial supply   - Proximal: branches from renal artery; middle: branches from gonadal, aorta, common iliac; distal: branches from internal iliac (superior/inferior vesical, uterine); rich segmental collateral supply. - Venous drainage   - Mirrors arteries to renal, gonadal, common iliac, and internal iliac veins. - Lymphatics   - Drain to lateral aortic (upper), common iliac (middle), and external/internal iliac (lower) nodes. - Nerves   - Visceral sensory and sympathetic fibers from renal, aortic, and hypogastric plexuses; parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic contributions to distal ureter. - Histology   - Mucosa: transitional epithelium; lamina propria; muscularis: inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layers (third outer longitudinal layer present in lower ureter in many descriptions); adventitia or serosa where applicable. - Physiology   - Peristaltic waves (generated by pacemaker regions in renal pelvis/upper ureter and modulated by autonomic input) propel urine to the bladder; passive valve-like function at ureterovesical junction prevents reflux.  4) Urinary bladder - Location & gross anatomy   - Subperitoneal in pelvis when empty; expands into abdomen when full. Apex, body, fundus (base), neck (continues as urethra). Trigone triangular area between ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice — smooth mucosa. - Arterial supply   - Superior vesical arteries (from umbilical/internal iliac), inferior vesical (males) or vaginal/uterine branches (females) from internal iliac. - Venous drainage   - Vesical venous plexus → internal iliac veins. - Lymphatics   - Drains to external, internal, and common iliac lymph nodes (and sacral nodes for the posterior bladder). - Nerves   - Autonomic control: sympathetic (hypogastric nerves T11–L2) — relaxes detrusor and contracts internal sphincter (storage); parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnics S2–S4) — contracts detrusor and relaxes internal sphincter (voiding). Somatic pudendal (S2–S4) controls external urethral sphincter (voluntary). - Histology   - Mucosa: transitional epithelium with rugae when empty. Lamina propria and a thick muscularis (detrusor) composed of interwoven smooth muscle fibers in multiple orientations. Neck contains internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle) and external sphincter is skeletal muscle. - Physiology   - Reservoir function with high compliance; coordinated filling (sympathetic, somatic tone maintained) and micturition reflex (parasympathetic-mediated detrusor contraction + voluntary relaxation of external sphincter) for storage and elimination of urine.  5) Urethra - Location & gross anatomy   - Conveys urine from bladder to exterior. Short in females (~4 cm), longer and segmented in males (~20 cm: prostatic, membranous, spongy/penile). - Arterial/venous/lymphatics/nerves   - Arterial supply from internal pudendal and vesical/vaginal branches; venous plexus to internal pudendal/internal iliac systems. Lymphatics: female proximal to internal iliac nodes, distal to superficial inguinal; male prostatic/membranous to internal iliac, distal penile to superficial inguinal. Innervation: somatic pudendal nerve for external sphincter and sensory; autonomic (pelvic splanchnic and hypogastric) for glandular/vascular components. - Histology   - Female: transitional epithelium proximally → stratified squamous distally; male: transitional/psuedostratified columnar in prostatic and membranous portions → stratified squamous in distal penile urethra; submucosal glands in male urethra (glands of Littre). - Physiology   - Conduit for urine (and semen in males); sphincteric control for continence (internal sphincter smooth muscle, external sphincter skeletal under voluntary control).  Key integrated physiologic points (textbook essentials) - The nephron (glomerular filtration + tubular processing) is the functional unit; renal blood flow and GFR are tightly regulated by autoregulation (myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback), sympathetic tone, and hormones (angiotensin II, natriuretic peptides). - Countercurrent multiplier (loop of Henle) and countercurrent exchanger (vasa recta) generate and preserve medullary osmotic gradient for urine concentration under ADH (vasopressin) control acting on collecting ducts (aquaporin insertion). - Renal endocrine functions: renin (blood pressure/Na regulation), erythropoietin (RBC production), activation of vitamin D (calcium homeostasis). - Lower urinary tract: hierarchical control between autonomic reflexes and somatic voluntary control enables coordinated storage and voiding. 5|93:	Below is a concise, textbook-style summary of the renal system organized by anatomic part, covering location, arterial and venous supply, nerves, key histology, and principal physiology.  1) Kidney (organ) - Location: Retroperitoneal at T12–L3 vertebral levels on either side of the vertebral column; right kidney is slightly lower. Medial hilum faces vertebral column. - Arteries: Renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta (just distal to the SMA). At the hilum each renal artery divides into anterior and posterior divisions (≈75% and 25% of flow) and then into 5 segmental arteries (end arteries). Segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular → afferent arterioles → glomerular capillaries. - Veins: Venous return parallels arteries in reverse: interlobular → arcuate → interlobar → renal vein → IVC. Left renal vein is longer and crosses anterior to the aorta. - Nerves: Renal plexus (predominantly sympathetic fibers from thoracic/least splanchnic and aorticorenal ganglia; some parasympathetic vagal fibers). Sympathetic input controls arteriolar tone and renin release; parasympathetic input is minor. - Histology: Cortex contains renal corpuscles (glomeruli with fenestrated capillaries, basement membrane and podocytes) and convoluted tubules. Medulla contains straight tubules and collecting ducts arranged in pyramids; papillae drain into minor calyces. Urothelium (transitional epithelium) lines the collecting system from calyces to ureter. - Physiology (organ-level): Filters plasma, produces concentrated urine, regulates volume/electrolytes/acid–base, synthesizes hormones (renin, erythropoietin) and activates vitamin D.  2) Renal collecting system (renal papilla → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter) - Location: Papilla at apex of each pyramid projects into a minor calyx; several minors join to form major calyces → renal pelvis at hilum → ureter. - Arteries/veins: Supplied by branches of renal artery (small intrarenal branches) and drained by intrarenal veins into the renal vein. Ureteric arterial supply derives from renal, gonadal, common iliac, and internal iliac arterial branches along its course; venous drainage parallels. - Nerves: Autonomic fibers from renal, aortic, and hypogastric plexuses; ureter has sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation regulating peristalsis. - Histology: Minor/major calyces, pelvis and ureter lined by transitional epithelium with lamina propria and muscularis. Ureter muscularis: inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle (with an additional outer longitudinal layer developing distally). - Physiology: Conveys urine by gravity and coordinated peristalsis; calyces/pelvis act as conduits and limited reservoirs; ureterovesical junction prevents reflux.  3) Nephron (functional unit) — main parts A. Renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman’s capsule) - Location: Renal cortex. - Blood supply: Afferent arteriole feeds glomerular capillaries; efferent arteriole drains them. - Nerves: Local autonomic modulation via renal plexus affecting arteriolar tone. - Histology: Fenestrated glomerular capillaries, glomerular basement membrane, podocytes with slit diaphragms, mesangial cells. - Physiology: Ultrafiltration of plasma driven by capillary hydrostatic and oncotic forces; determines GFR and filters water + small solutes while retaining cells and most proteins.  B. Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) - Location: Cortex, immediately downstream of Bowman’s capsule. - Blood supply: Peritubular capillaries from efferent arteriole. - Histology: Simple cuboidal epithelium with tall microvilli (brush border), abundant mitochondria. - Physiology: Reabsorbs ~65–70% of filtered Na+ and water, nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids, substantial bicarbonate; secretion of organic acids and drugs.  C. Loop of Henle (descending limb, thin ascending, thick ascending limb) - Location: Descends into medulla (vasa recta run alongside). - Blood supply: Vasa recta (efferent-derived) supply medullary interstitium; countercurrent exchange. - Histology: Thin segments lined by simple squamous epithelium; thick ascending limb lined by cuboidal epithelium with many mitochondria. - Physiology: Countercurrent multiplier: descending limb highly permeable to water (not solute), thin/thick ascending limb reabsorbs NaCl but is impermeable to water (thick ascending uses active transport via NKCC2). Creates and preserves medullary osmotic gradient for urine concentration.  D. Distal convoluted tubule (DCT) - Location: Cortex, after thick ascending limb. - Blood supply: Peritubular capillaries. - Histology: Simple cuboidal epithelium with fewer microvilli; macula densa region where DCT contacts afferent arteriole. - Physiology: Fine-tuning of NaCl reabsorption (thiazide-sensitive NCC), Ca2+ reabsorption under PTH; participates in tubuloglomerular feedback via macula densa to regulate GFR and renin release.  E. Collecting duct (cortical → medullary → papillary ducts) - Location: Cortex to papilla. - Blood supply: Vasa recta and medullary capillaries supply surrounding interstitium. - Histology: Principal cells (Na+ and water channels, responsive to ADH and aldosterone) and intercalated cells (type A and B for acid–base handling). - Physiology: Final concentration/volume adjustment. ADH (vasopressin) increases water permeability via aquaporin-2 in principal cells to concentrate urine; aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion; intercalated cells secrete H+ or HCO3- to regulate acid–base.  4) Vascular architecture and clinical implication - End-artery arrangement: Segmental renal arteries are end arteries with minimal intrarenal anastomoses; occlusion causes ischemic infarct of that segment. - Medullary blood supply: Vasa recta supply inner cortex/medulla and preserve osmotic gradient via countercurrent exchange; medulla is relatively hypoxic compared with cortex.  5) Lymphatics and minor autonomic notes - Lymph: Drains to lateral (para‑aortic) lymph nodes at renal artery origin. - Autonomic effects: Sympathetic stimulation vasoconstricts afferent (and especially efferent) arterioles, reduces renal blood flow and GFR, and stimulates renin release; parasympathetic effects on renal function are limited.  This summary follows standard textbook organization: anatomical relations and positions, arterial/venous/nerve supply, basic histological structure of each segment, and their principal physiological roles. Collecting ducts in the renal pyramids participate in final water and urea handling (ADH-sensitive).  3) Ureter - Location / relations   - Muscular retroperitoneal tubes (~25–30 cm) from renal pelvis to the bladder, passing over iliac vessels into the pelvis. Three physiologic narrowing sites: pelvi-ureteric junction, crossing of iliac vessels, ureterovesical junction.  - Arterial supply   - Multiple small arterial sources: proximal ureter from renal arteries, middle ureter from gonadal and aortic branches, distal ureter from common/internal iliac and superior/inferior vesical arteries. Rich longitudinal anastomoses.  - Venous drainage & lymphatics   - Veins follow arteries to renal, gonadal, and iliac veins. Lies in pelvis when empty and rises into abdomen when full.  - Arterial supply   - Superior vesical arteries (from umbilical branch of internal iliac) and inferior vesical artery in males (or vaginal artery in females); additional small branches from obturator/internal pudendal.  - Venous drainage & lymphatics   - Vesical venous plexus drains to internal iliac veins. Sympathetic (hypogastric plexus, T11–L2) relaxes detrusor and contracts internal sphincter (storage). Somatic pudendal nerve (S2–S4) innervates external urethral sphincter (voluntary control).  - Histology   - Mucosa lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium) with lamina propria; muscularis = detrusor muscle (interwoven smooth muscle bundles, often described in three layers). Adventitia/serosa superiorly where peritoneum covers.  - Physiology   - Storage phase: bladder compliance allows filling at low pressure; sympathetic and somatic tone maintain continence. Voiding (micturition): coordinated parasympathetic-driven detrusor contraction, relaxation of internal sphincter (autonomic) and voluntary relaxation of external sphincter.  5) Urethra - Location / relations   - Tubular outlet from bladder to exterior. Male urethra is longer (~20 cm) with prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts; female urethra is short (~4 cm), opening anterior to vaginal opening.  - Arterial supply & venous drainage   - Blood supply from internal pudendal, inferior vesical, vaginal/prostatic branches; venous plexuses drain to internal pudendal and internal iliac veins.  - Lymphatics   - Drain to internal pudendal and deep inguinal nodes (distal urethra), and internal/external iliac nodes depending on level and sex.  - Nerves   - Somatic innervation to external urethral sphincter via pudendal nerve (S2–S4). Autonomic fibers modulate internal sphincter tone (sympathetic) and mucosal blood flow.  - Histology   - Proximal urethra lined by transitional epithelium (near bladder) → columnar/pseudostratified in mid portions → stratified squamous epithelium distally (especially near external meatus).  - Physiology   - Conduit for urine; sphincteric mechanisms (internal smooth muscle sphincter and external striated sphincter) govern continence together with pelvic floor muscles.  Key integrated points (textbook essentials) - Intrarenal arterial branches are end-arteries: obstruction of a segmental artery produces ischemia of that renal segment (no collateral supply). - Countercurrent multiplier (loop of Henle) plus vasa recta countercurrent exchange are essential for urine concentration. - Juxtaglomerular apparatus senses renal perfusion and NaCl delivery to regulate renin release and GFR (tubuloglomerular feedback). - Autonomic control: kidney vascular tone and renin are sympathetically modulated; bladder emptying requires parasympathetic activation and coordinated somatic relaxation. - Urothelium lines all urine-transporting structures from minor calyces to proximal urethra and is specialized for stretch and impermeability. Bean-shaped with anterior/posterior surfaces, lateral convex and medial hilum. Internal: cortex (outer) and medulla (pyramids, papillae); minor calyces collect from papillae → major calyces → renal pelvis → ureter. - Arteries/veins   - Renal arteries from abdominal aorta. At hilum each divides into anterior and posterior divisions → segmental arteries (end arteries; no intra-renal anastomoses). Segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular → afferent arterioles. Venous drainage parallels arteries but interlobular → arcuate → interlobar → renal vein; renal veins drain to IVC (left renal vein longer). - Nerves   - Primarily sympathetic fibers from the renal plexus (preganglionic from T10–L1 via splanchnics and aorticorenal/celiac plexuses); sparse parasympathetic (vagal) input of uncertain functional importance. Visceral afferents convey pain (referred to T10–L2 dermatomes). - Histology (gross tissue architecture)   - Cortex contains renal corpuscles (glomeruli + Bowman's capsule), proximal and distal convoluted tubules. Medulla contains loops of Henle and collecting ducts arranged in pyramids. Collecting ducts converge at papilla; urothelium lines minor calyces/pelvis/ureter. - Physiology (principal functions)   - Filtration at glomerulus (glomerular capillary filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, podocytes). Tubular reabsorption and secretion along PCT (major bulk reabsorption: ~65% Na+ and water, all filtered glucose/amino acids), loop of Henle (countercurrent multiplier; thin limbs passive, thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs NaCl and is impermeable to water), DCT (fine-tuning, regulated Na+ reabsorption), collecting duct (ADH-regulated water reabsorption; aldosterone-sensitive Na+ reabsorption). Efferent arterioles supply peritubular capillaries (cortex) and vasa recta (medulla) for exchange and concentration. Autoregulation of renal blood flow and GFR via myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback; endocrine roles (renin secretion by juxtaglomerular cells, EPO from interstitial cells, vitamin D activation).  2) Nephron (functional unit) - Anatomy   - Two main types: cortical (short loops) and juxtamedullary (long loops into medulla). Composed of renal corpuscle → PCT → loop of Henle → DCT → collecting duct. - Histology   - Renal corpuscle: glomerular capillary tuft with specialized podocytes; Bowman's capsule parietal epithelium. PCT: simple cuboidal epithelium with a prominent brush border. Thin limb: simple squamous. Thick ascending limb and DCT: cuboidal epithelium (less brush border). Collecting ducts: cuboidal/columnar epithelium; principal and intercalated cells. - Physiology   - Filtration (plasma → primary urine), selective reabsorption (water, electrolytes, nutrients), secretion (H+, K+, organic ions), generation of osmotic medullary gradient (countercurrent multiplier and vasa recta countercurrent exchanger) to concentrate urine. Juxtaglomerular apparatus mediates renin release in response to perfusion/NaCl delivery.  3) Minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis - Location/anatomy   - Minor calyx cups papilla; several minor → major calyx → renal pelvis (funnel) continuous with ureter at ureteropelvic junction. - Arteries/veins   - Supplied by branches of the renal artery (segmental/interlobar) and smaller peri-pelvic branches; venous drainage to renal vein. - Nerves   - Visceral autonomic fibers from the renal/ureteric plexuses (sympathetic and parasympathetic components). - Histology   - Lined by urothelium (transitional epithelium) over lamina propria. - Physiology   - Passive collection conduits; renal pelvis initiates peristaltic waves transmitted into ureter; no significant absorption/secretion.  4) Ureter - Location/anatomy   - Muscular tube ~25–30 cm, retroperitoneal, runs from renal pelvis to urinary bladder. Three physiological constrictions: ureteropelvic junction, pelvic brim (crossing iliac vessels), ureterovesical junction. - Arteries/veins   - Multiple segmental arterial sources along its course: proximal ureter from renal artery branches; middle from gonadal and aortic/iliac branches; distal from superior/inferior vesical and internal iliac branches. Venous drainage mirrors arteries to renal/gonadal/internal iliac veins. - Nerves   - Ureteric plexus: sympathetic fibers from T11–L2 (pain and modulation of peristalsis) and parasympathetic inputs (vagal proximally, pelvic splanchnics S2–S4 distally). Visceral afferents refer pain to T11–L2. - Histology   - Mucosa: urothelium; muscularis: inner longitudinal + outer circular smooth muscle (third outer longitudinal layer present in lower third); adventitia or serosa. - Physiology   - Peristaltic transport of urine from kidney to bladder; intrinsic pacemaker in renal pelvis and nervous modulation; passive one-way flow aided by oblique intramural course at bladder to prevent reflux.  5) Urinary bladder - Location/anatomy   - Extraperitoneal pelvic organ; in adults when empty lies in pelvis, expands into abdomen when full. Trigone demarcated by ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice. - Arteries/veins   - Superior vesical arteries (from umbilical/internal iliac); inferior vesical (male) or vaginal branches (female); venous plexus drains to internal iliac veins. - Nerves   - Parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnics S2–S4): detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation for voiding. Sympathetic (hypogastric T11–L2): detrusor relaxation and internal sphincter contraction for storage. Somatic (pudendal S2–S4) to external urethral sphincter (voluntary control). - Histology   - Mucosa: urothelium with rugae when empty. Submucosa/lamina propria. Detrusor muscle: three interlaced smooth muscle layers. Internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle) and external sphincter (skeletal). - Physiology   - Urine storage (compliance, sympathetic tone maintains continence) and micturition reflex (parasympathetic-mediated detrusor contraction coordinated with voluntary relaxation of external sphincter). Integration in pontine micturition center and higher centers.  6) Urethra - Anatomy   - Short in female (~4 cm) and longer in male (~20 cm) with prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts. - Arteries/veins   - Blood supply from internal pudendal, inferior vesical, vaginal/prostatic branches; venous drainage to corresponding plexuses. - Nerves   - Somatic pudendal nerve to external sphincter (voluntary control); autonomic fibers modulate glandular and smooth muscle function. - Histology   - Transitional epithelium near bladder → pseudostratified columnar → stratified squamous distally in parts exposed to outside. - Physiology   - Conduit for urine expulsion; continence maintained by external sphincter innervated by pudendal nerve.  Key textbook points to remember - Renal segmental arteries are end arteries — occlusion causes infarction of the supplied segment. The renal artery/vein/ureter relations at the hilum are (anterior → posterior) renal vein, renal artery, pelvis/ureter. - Nephrons are the functional units; kidney function integrates filtration, selective reabsorption/secretion, concentration (countercurrent mechanisms), and endocrine roles (renin, EPO, vitamin D activation). - Urothelium lines the collecting system and bladder and is specialized to accommodate stretch while maintaining a barrier. 10|93:	Below is a compact, textbook-style summary of the renal (urinary) system organized by anatomic part. For each part I give: usual location, arterial/venous supply and innervation, main histology, and core physiology/function.  1) Kidneys (paired) - Location: retroperitoneal, T12–L3 vertebral region; right kidney usually ~1 rib level lower than left; medial hilum (usually at L1) faces medially. - Arteries/veins/nerves:   - Arteries: single renal artery from abdominal aorta (just distal to SMA); divides at hilum into anterior/posterior divisions → 5 segmental arteries → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular → afferent arterioles.   - Veins: interlobular → arcuate → interlobar → renal vein → IVC; left renal vein longer and receives left gonadal and left suprarenal veins.   - Nerves: renal plexus (sympathetic fibers from thoracic/lumbar splanchnic nerves—T10–L2 levels; parasympathetic vagal fibers variably present). Sympathetic input regulates renal vascular tone and renin release. - Histology (gross/microscopic organization):   - Cortex: glomeruli, proximal/distal convoluted tubules, cortical collecting ducts.   - Medulla: straight tubules (loops of Henle) and collecting ducts arranged into pyramids; papilla at apex drains into minor calyx.   - Vasculature: glomerular capillary loops with fenestrated endothelium; Bowman’s capsule (parietal epithelium); mesangium. - Physiology:   - Primary functions: filtration of plasma (glomerular filtration), selective reabsorption and secretion along tubules, urine concentration via countercurrent mechanisms, endocrine functions (renin, erythropoietin, calcitriol activation).   - Autoregulation of renal blood flow and GFR via myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback; juxtaglomerular apparatus (JG cells secrete renin → RAAS).  2) Nephron (functional unit) — give major segments (location, histology, physiology) - Renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman’s capsule)   - Location: renal cortex.   - Histology: fenestrated glomerular endothelium, glomerular basement membrane, podocytes with slit diaphragms; parietal layer of Bowman’s capsule is simple squamous epithelium.   - Physiology: plasma ultrafiltration driven by hydrostatic/oncotic pressures; filtration barrier selectively filters water and small solutes while retaining cells and large proteins. - Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)   - Location: cortex (cortical labyrinth around glomeruli).   - Histology: simple cuboidal epithelium with prominent brush border (microvilli), abundant mitochondria, basolateral infoldings.   - Physiology: bulk reabsorption (~65–70% Na+ and water), complete reabsorption of glucose and amino acids, secretion of organic anions/cations. - Loop of Henle   - Location: descends into outer/inner medulla; long loops characteristic of juxtamedullary nephrons.   - Histology: thin limbs (simple squamous), thick ascending limb (simple cuboidal, many mitochondria).   - Physiology: countercurrent multiplier — thin descending limb permeable to water, thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs NaCl (NKCC2) and is impermeable to water; establishes and maintains hyperosmotic medullary interstitium. - Distal convoluted tubule (DCT)   - Location: cortex (adjacent to glomerulus for some nephrons); macula densa forms part of JGA.   - Histology: cuboidal cells, fewer microvilli than PCT, mitochondria for active transport.   - Physiology: NaCl reabsorption (NCC), Ca2+ reabsorption under PTH control; contributes to fine-tuning of electrolyte balance. - Collecting duct system (cortical collecting ducts → medullary collecting ducts → papillary ducts)   - Location: cortex to medulla to papilla.   - Histology: principal cells (simple cuboidal → columnar in inner medulla) and intercalated cells (type A/B) for acid–base regulation.   - Physiology: principal cells respond to ADH (vasopressin) to insert aquaporin-2 channels for facultative water reabsorption; aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion; collecting ducts concentrate urine as fluid passes through hyperosmotic medulla. - Vasa recta   - Location: alongside loops of Henle in medulla.   - Histology: straight capillary loops.   - Physiology: countercurrent exchanger that preserves medullary osmotic gradient while supplying oxygen/nutrients.  3) Renal pelvis, major and minor calyces - Location: renal sinus; minor calyx collects renal papilla effluent → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter. - Arteries/veins/nerves: branches from renal artery/vein and peri-pelvic vessels; innervated by sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers via renal/ureteric plexuses. - Histology: urothelium (transitional epithelium) over lamina propria; muscularis layer (smooth muscle) of variable arrangement. - Physiology: passive collection and funneling of urine from papillae to ureter.  4) Ureter - Location: retroperitoneal tubular conduit from renal pelvis at L1 descending to posterolateral bladder wall (crosses pelvic brim near bifurcation of common iliac). - Arterial/venous supply:   - Arterial: proximal ureter from renal artery; mid-ureter from gonadal and aortic/iliac branches; distal ureter from common/internal iliac and superior/inferior vesical arteries.   - Venous drainage parallels arteries to renal, gonadal and internal iliac veins. - Nerves: sympathetic (T11–L2) and parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic S2–S4) fibers; visceral afferents transmit pain (stone pain referred to T11–L2 dermatomes). - Histology: mucosa with transitional epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis (inner longitudinal and outer circular proximally; distal third has additional outer longitudinal layer), adventitia. - Physiology: peristaltic waves generated by ureteric smooth muscle and pacemaker cells propel urine to bladder; one‑way flow aided by oblique intramural insertion into bladder preventing reflux.  5) Urinary bladder - Location: pelvic cavity (empty); rises into abdomen when full. - Arteries/veins/nerves:   - Arterial: superior vesical arteries (from umbilical artery), inferior vesical in males (or vaginal/uterine branches in females); additional pubic branches as applicable.   - Venous: vesical venous plexus → internal iliac veins.   - Nerves: sympathetic (hypogastric plexus T11–L2) for bladder neck/internal sphincter tone and relaxation of detrusor during filling; parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic S2–S4) for detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation during voiding; somatic (pudendal S2–S4) to external urethral sphincter. - Histology: urothelium, lamina propria, thick muscularis (detrusor: interlacing smooth muscle bundles), adventitia (or serosa superiorly). - Physiology: reservoir function (storage phase under sympathetic and somatic control) and micturition reflex (parasympathetic-driven detrusor contraction + voluntary relaxation of external sphincter).  6) Urethra - Location: female short (~4 cm) from bladder neck to external meatus; male longer (~18–20 cm) with prostatic, membranous, and spongy/penile parts. - Arteries/veins/nerves: arterial supply from internal pudendal and inferior vesical/vaginal branches; venous plexuses drain to internal iliac system; somatic motor via pudendal nerve to external sphincter; autonomic fibers regulate internal sphincter (male) and urethral smooth muscle. - Histology: transitional epithelium proximally (bladder neck/prostatic urethra), then columnar, then stratified squamous near external opening (especially in female distal urethra and male fossa navicularis). - Physiology: conduit for urine elimination; external urethral sphincter provides voluntary continence.  Key physiologic systems and clinical notes (textbook essentials) - Filtration and clearance: GFR determined by net filtration pressure and filtration coefficient; renal plasma flow and filtration fraction clinically important. - Countercurrent multiplier/exchanger (loop of Henle + vasa recta) allow urine concentration; ADH regulates water permeability of collecting ducts. - Tubuloglomerular feedback / autoregulation keep GFR stable over a range of arterial pressures. - Juxtaglomerular apparatus / RAAS: renin → angiotensin II (efferent arteriole constriction, aldosterone release) → increased Na+ retention and BP. - Clinical vascular note: segmental renal arteries are end arteries (little collateral supply) — infarction can result from single-branch occlusion. - Lymphatics: kidney and ureter drain to lateral (para‑aortic/aortic) nodes; bladder drains to external/internal iliac nodes.
